The rules that apply to everything in this document

All material of this course is created for one purpose: teaching defensive cybersecurity. It shows how to protect systems, never how to attack the systems of others. By reading or using any part of it, you accept the entire Legal Notice, Disclaimer, and Acceptable Use Policy — Version 1.0 (effective August 29, 2026), reproduced in full at the end of this document.

Learning objectives

At the end of these two classes, you can

  1. Define subject, operation, object, identity, authentication, authorization, accounting, permission and privilege, and place each in the AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) model.
  2. Apply the principles of least privilege and need-to-know to the role table of NorthMaple Accounting Inc. and measure their effect.
  3. Create user accounts and role groups on a Windows machine and on a Linux machine, and export the memberships as evidence.
  4. Describe the joiner, mover and leaver procedures and run an access review against a role table.
  5. Set NTFS (New Technology File System) and share permissions on a folder so that one role reaches its data and every other role is refused.
  6. Read and set Linux ownership and permission bits, and write a restricted sudo rule.
  7. List eight techniques that secure access to sensitive data and name the lab in which each is applied.
  8. Name six malware families, the weakness of access control each one abuses, and one detection and one prevention measure for each.

Class 3 — Wednesday, September 2

Network Access Control and Security — part 1

Lesson 1 covers the decisions of access control: who may do what, on which system, and how that decision is kept true over time. Four sub-topics: the vocabulary of privilege and access management (1.1), the two principles that size every permission (1.2), how Windows and Linux represent users, groups and roles (1.3), and the processes that grant, review and remove access (1.4). Everything is applied to NorthMaple Accounting Inc., the fictional company of every lab and of the Final Project.

1.1 Privilege and access management: who may do what, on which system 10 min

Slides 7–10 of the deck — 7 1.1 Access control: subject, operation, object (1/2); 8 1.1 Models and the access matrix (2/2); 9 1.1 The access matrix of NorthMaple Accounting Inc.; 10 1.1 Example and script — nm_access_matrix.py
Slide 7Slide 8Slide 9Slide 10

Access control is the set of rules and mechanisms that decide whether a subject (a user account, a service, or a program acting for a user) may perform an operation (read, write, execute, delete, change permissions) on an object (a file, a folder, a database, a network device, a service). Every access control decision therefore has exactly three parts: the subject, the operation, and the object. Cyber defense starts by writing these decisions down before any system is configured.

Four terms must be kept separate, because each one is a different process on the machine:

  • Identity — the digital representation of a person or of a program on a system. On Windows and on Linux it is a user account with a unique identifier: a SID (Security Identifier) on Windows, a UID (User Identifier) on Linux.
  • Authentication — the process that verifies that the entity using an identity is the one it claims to be (a password, a hardware key, a one-time code from an application).
  • Authorization — the decision, taken after a successful authentication, of what the identity may do. Permissions and privileges apply at this step.
  • Accounting (also called auditing) — the recording of what the identity actually did, so that access can be reviewed later. Together, the three processes form the AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) model.

Permission and privilege are two different things. A permission is a right attached to an object: "the group accountants may modify the folder ClientRecords". A privilege is a right attached to an identity and valid on the whole system: "the account g.lopez may install software", "may change the system time", "may take ownership of any file". Windows calls privileges user rights; Linux grants most of them through the root account, reached in a controlled way with sudo (Class 4).

Privilege and access management — in the industry, IAM (Identity and Access Management) — is the organized process by which an organization (1) decides which roles exist, (2) decides which permissions and privileges each role needs on each system, (3) creates the identities and the groups that implement that decision, (4) reviews the result at fixed intervals, and (5) removes access as soon as it is no longer needed. The written output of step (2) is the access matrix: a table with one row per role, one column per system (or per object), and, in each cell, the highest privilege level the role may hold. This course uses four privilege levels: NONE (no account, no access), READ (look only), USE (read and write the data of the role), and ADMIN (change the configuration of the system itself).

Three access control models describe how the decision is organized:

  • DAC (Discretionary Access Control) — the owner of an object decides who may access it. It is the default model of NTFS (New Technology File System) permissions and of Linux file permissions.
  • MAC (Mandatory Access Control) — a central policy, not the owner, decides: the system compares security labels carried by subjects and by objects (SELinux and AppArmor on Linux, Mandatory Integrity Control on Windows). Awareness level only in this course.
  • RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) — permissions are attached to roles, roles are implemented as groups, and an identity receives access by being placed in a group. Every lab of this course uses this model: the role table of NorthMaple Accounting Inc. is an RBAC design.

Why this is a layer of defense-in-depth. Access control limits what an attacker can do after another defense has failed. The perimeter firewall (LAB_05) decides which traffic enters the network; access control decides what an identity may touch once it is inside. When every identity may touch everything, the perimeter is the only layer, and defense-in-depth does not exist. The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls introduced in Class 2 dedicate two controls to this layer: Control 5 (Account Management) and Control 6 (Access Control Management) — see cisecurity.org/controls. The formal definitions used above follow the glossary of the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Computer Security Resource Center: csrc.nist.gov/glossary.

Real-life example — Build the access matrix of NorthMaple Accounting Inc.

Task: Write, before any account exists, the table that states which privilege level each role holds on each system of the company, and check it against one rule: no user role administers a server-zone system.

Relation to the lecture: This is step (2) of privilege and access management. The matrix is the written access control decision (subject = role, operation = privilege level, object = system) that every later configuration must follow.

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: LAB_02 part 1 uses this matrix to decide the group memberships; the matrix and its check are evidence for Chapter 2 (Access control) of the Final Project and of the Course Procedure Manual. The systems in the columns are the systems of the LAB_01 network diagram (Chapter 1).

Gina Lopez (fictional), the new IT administrator of NorthMaple Accounting Inc., receives the request "give an account to everybody before Monday". She does not open a single administration console. She first lists the six systems of the LAB_01 diagram, the five roles of the role table, and fills one cell per role and per system with NONE, READ, USE or ADMIN. She then verifies one rule that applies to every small company: only the IT administrator holds ADMIN on the firewall, on the web server, on the file server and on the VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway. The manager signs the table. The signed table goes into the manual; every account and group created in LAB_02 is traced back to one cell of this table.

Deliverable of this example: northmaple_access_matrix.csv — the access matrix (one row per role), plus the printed result of the policy check, pasted as evidence into Chapter 2 of the manual.

Illustration script — nm_access_matrix.py (Python 3)

Task: The script builds the access matrix from the role table, prints it, checks the rule “no user role administers a server-zone system”, and saves the matrix as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file for the manual.

Relation to the lecture: It turns the three parts of an access control decision (role, privilege level, system) into a table that can be verified automatically — the written basis of RBAC.

ready
# Load the csv module: the finished matrix is written to a file that goes into the Course Procedure Manual.import csv # The six systems of NorthMaple Accounting Inc. that appear in the LAB_01 network diagram (Chapter 1 of the Final Project).SYSTEMS = ["Firewall", "Web server (DMZ)", "File server", "Windows workstation", "Linux workstation", "VPN gateway"] # The four privilege levels of this course, from nothing to full control of the system itself.LEVELS = ["NONE", "READ", "USE", "ADMIN"] # The role table of the company: for each role, the privilege level it needs on every system, in the order of SYSTEMS - and nothing more.ROLES = {    "Administrator (IT)": ["ADMIN", "ADMIN", "ADMIN", "ADMIN", "ADMIN", "ADMIN"],    "Accountant":         ["NONE",  "NONE",  "USE",   "USE",   "USE",   "NONE"],    "Technician":         ["NONE",  "NONE",  "USE",   "ADMIN", "ADMIN", "NONE"],    "Receptionist":       ["NONE",  "NONE",  "USE",   "USE",   "NONE",  "NONE"],    "Remote worker":      ["NONE",  "NONE",  "USE",   "NONE",  "NONE",  "USE"],} # The systems on which only the IT administrator may hold ADMIN: servers and perimeter devices are never administered from a user role.SERVER_ZONE = {"Firewall", "Web server (DMZ)", "File server", "VPN gateway"} # A function that returns the privilege level of one role on one system, so that the matrix can be read cell by cell.def level(role, system):    # The position of the system in SYSTEMS is the position of its level in the list of the role.    return ROLES[role][SYSTEMS.index(system)] # Print the header row of the matrix: the word ROLE, then one column title per system (shortened to 14 characters).print("ROLE".ljust(20) + " | " + " | ".join(s[:14].ljust(14) for s in SYSTEMS)) # Walk through every role: this loop prints the "who may do what, on which system" table, one row per role.for role in ROLES:    # Build and print the row: the role name followed by its privilege level on each system.    print(role.ljust(20) + " | " + " | ".join(level(role, s).ljust(14) for s in SYSTEMS)) # Policy check: collect every (role, system) pair where a role other than the IT administrator holds ADMIN on a server-zone system.violations = [(r, s) for r in ROLES for s in SERVER_ZONE if r != "Administrator (IT)" and level(r, s) == "ADMIN"] # Report the result of the check in one line that can be pasted as evidence into the manual.print("Policy check:", "PASS - no user role administers a server-zone system" if not violations else "FAIL - " + str(violations)) # Save the matrix as a CSV file: this file is the access-matrix deliverable of LAB_02 (Chapter 2 evidence).with open("northmaple_access_matrix.csv", "w", newline="") as f:    # Create the writer object that formats rows for the CSV file.    w = csv.writer(f)    # Write the header row: the word Role followed by the system names.    w.writerow(["Role"] + SYSTEMS)    # Write one row per role with its six privilege levels.    for role in ROLES:        w.writerow([role] + ROLES[role])

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Line by line, the script first imports csv, the standard module that writes comma-separated files.
  2. SYSTEMS lists the six objects of the decision; LEVELS lists the four privilege levels the course allows.
  3. ROLES is the access matrix itself: the key is the role (the subject), the list holds one privilege level per system, in the same order as SYSTEMS.
  4. SERVER_ZONE names the systems that only the IT administrator may administer; it is the rule the script will verify.
  5. The function level(role, system) looks up one cell of the matrix, so the rest of the script never depends on list positions.
  6. The two print blocks display the matrix as a table: header first, then one row per role — this is the screenshot for the manual.
  7. The violations line is a list comprehension: it keeps every (role, system) pair that breaks the rule. An empty list means PASS.
  8. The last block writes the same matrix to northmaple_access_matrix.csv; the file is attached to Chapter 2 of the manual and reused in LAB_02 to create the groups.
  9. To run it in the isolated laboratory: python3 nm_access_matrix.py on the Linux workstation, or py nm_access_matrix.py on the Windows workstation with Python installed.

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

What three elements does every access control decision contain?
A subject (who), an operation (which action), and an object (on which resource). Example: the group accountants (subject) may modify (operation) the folder ClientRecords (object).
What is the difference between a permission and a privilege?
A permission is attached to an object (a folder, a file, a share). A privilege — a user right on Windows — is attached to an identity and applies to the whole system (install software, take ownership, change the time).
What does AAA stand for, and in which order do the three processes run?
Authentication (prove the identity), then Authorization (decide what it may do), then Accounting (record what it did).
What is an access matrix?
A table with one row per role, one column per system or object, and, in each cell, the highest privilege level (NONE, READ, USE, ADMIN) the role may hold.
Which access control model does the NorthMaple role table implement?
RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) (Role-Based Access Control): permissions are attached to groups that represent roles; a user receives access only through group membership.

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. Which statement describes authorization?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Authorization is the step that comes after authentication succeeds.

✗ Proving that the password typed by the user is correct. — That is authentication: verifying that the entity is who it claims to be.

✓ Deciding what an authenticated identity may do on the system. — Correct: authorization is the decision about the operations the identity may perform on the objects.

✗ Recording which files the identity opened during the day. — That is accounting (auditing): the record of what the identity did.

✗ Creating a new user account for a new employee. — Creating an identity is account provisioning, part of the identity life cycle (section 1.4), not the authorization decision.

Q2. In the access matrix, the cell (Receptionist, File server) contains USE. What does this mean?one answer — 4 options

Hint: USE is the level between READ and ADMIN: read and write the data of the role only.

✗ The receptionist may administer the file server. — Administration of the system is ADMIN, reserved to the IT administrator on every server-zone system.

✓ The receptionist may read and write only in the folder of the reception role. — Correct: USE means read and write access to the data of the role, here the front-desk folder, and nothing else.

✗ The receptionist has no account on the file server. — No account at all is the level NONE.

✗ The receptionist may reset the passwords of the accountants. — Resetting other users' passwords is an administrative privilege, not part of USE.

Q3. Which of the following is a privilege (a user right), not a permission?one answer — 4 options

Hint: A privilege is attached to the identity and applies everywhere on the system.

✗ Modify on D:\NorthMaple\ClientRecords. — Modify on a folder is a permission attached to that object.

✗ Read on /srv/northmaple/techdocs. — Read on a folder is a permission attached to that object.

✓ The right to install software on the workstation. — Correct: installing software is a system-wide right held by the identity (or its group), not a right on one object.

✗ List folder contents on the front-desk share. — List folder contents is an NTFS (New Technology File System) permission on one folder.

Q4. Why is access control considered a layer of defense-in-depth?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Think about what happens after the perimeter has been passed.

✗ Because it replaces the network firewall. — It does not replace the firewall; it is a second, independent layer behind it.

✓ Because it limits what an identity can reach after another layer has already failed. — Correct: when the perimeter is passed or one account is compromised, access control decides how far the damage can extend.

✗ Because it encrypts the traffic between the zones. — Encryption of traffic is the role of VPNs and TLS (Transport Layer Security) (LAB_06), not of access control.

✗ Because it detects malware signatures. — Signature detection is the role of antivirus software and of the IDS (Intrusion Detection System) (LAB_04).

Q5. Which of the following are steps of privilege and access management as defined in this section? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: The definition lists five steps, from the decision to the removal.

✓ Decide which roles exist in the organization. — Step (1) of the process.

✓ Decide which permissions and privileges each role needs on each system. — Step (2): the access matrix.

✗ Install an intrusion detection system on the network. — Detection is the subject of LAB_04, a different layer.

✓ Create the identities and the groups that implement the decision. — Step (3): the technical implementation.

✓ Review the result at fixed intervals. — Step (4): the access review.

✗ Configure the VPN gateway. — The VPN (Virtual Private Network) is a secure-communication layer (LAB_06), not part of access management.

Q6. Which items are objects in an access control decision? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Objects are the resources being accessed; subjects are the identities that access them.

✓ The folder ClientRecords on the file server. — A folder is a resource: an object.

✗ The account a.tremblay. — An account is an identity: a subject.

✓ The management page of the pfSense firewall. — A management interface is a resource that a subject accesses: an object.

✗ The operation 'delete'. — Delete is the operation, the second part of the decision, not the object.

✓ A table in the accounting database. — A database table is a resource: an object.

✗ The group accountants. — A group is a collection of subjects, used to assign permissions; it is not the resource being accessed.

1.2 The principles of least privilege and need-to-know access control 10 min

Slides 11–14 of the deck — 11 1.2 Least privilege (1/2); 12 1.2 Need-to-know and separation of duties (2/2); 13 1.2 Reach of one infected account; 14 1.2 Example — nm_least_privilege_reach.py
Slide 11Slide 12Slide 13Slide 14

The principle of least privilege states that every identity — a user, a service, a program — holds only the permissions and privileges strictly required to perform its assigned task, for the shortest time required, and nothing more. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) control catalogue SP 800-53 states it as control AC-6, "Least Privilege" (csrc.nist.gov — least privilege). Three practical consequences follow:

  • Daily work is never performed with an administrative account. An administrator has two accounts: one for e-mail and documents, one — used only for the administrative task — that holds the privileges.
  • A permission is granted to the role (the group), not to the person; a person receives access by joining the role.
  • A permission that is no longer needed is removed. The accumulation of permissions that were never removed is called privilege creep; it is measured and corrected by the access review (section 1.4).

Need-to-know is a second, independent principle: a subject receives access to a piece of information only if that information is required for the subject's current task, even when the subject's privilege level would technically allow the access. Least privilege limits the level of access; need-to-know limits the scope of the information. Example: two accountants hold the same privilege level (USE on the file server), yet the folder of client A is readable only by the accountant assigned to client A. That is need-to-know applied inside one privilege level. Need-to-know requires a data classification: each piece of information carries a level (for NorthMaple: public, internal, confidential) and confidential data is reachable only by the roles listed for it.

Separation of duties completes the two principles: a sensitive operation is divided so that no single identity can complete it alone (the accountant who prepares a payment is not the one who approves it; the administrator who creates an account is not the one who approves the request). Awareness level in this course.

The measurable effect. A program never obtains more rights than the account that started it, unless it exploits a vulnerability. Malware delivered by a phishing e-mail therefore runs with the permissions and privileges of the user who opened the attachment. The number of objects that account can reach is the number of objects the malware can read, modify, or encrypt. Least privilege is consequently the layer that directly reduces the impact of phishing, Trojans, and ransomware — rows 1, 3, 8 and 10 of the resilience assessment template of the Final Project (Chapter 7).

The same principle in physical access control. In the NorthMaple office, the receptionist holds a key for the front door and for the reception desk, but not for the archive room; the archive key is held by the accountants, and the server room key only by the IT administrator. The design question is identical to the one asked for files: for each key (permission), which role needs it to do its job?

How to apply the two principles, in order: (1) start every role at NONE on every system; (2) add the minimum level that the task needs, one cell at a time, with a one-sentence justification; (3) implement the level through a group, never through an individual account; (4) for administrative tasks, use elevation for the duration of the task only (UAC (User Account Control) on Windows, sudo on Linux); (5) review at fixed intervals and remove what is no longer used. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security lists "restrict administrative privileges" among its top ten security actions for organizations: cyber.gc.ca — Top 10 IT security actions.

Real-life example — Measure the damage one infected account can cause under two configurations

Task: Count how many folders of the NorthMaple file server a program started by the receptionist can reach, first when every user is a member of every group and of the administrators, then when the role table is applied.

Relation to the lecture: The count is the measurable effect of least privilege: the smaller the set of permissions of the account, the smaller the set of objects the malware started by that account can reach.

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: LAB_02 part 1 asks for least-privilege group memberships; the two counts of this example are the justification sentence of that choice in Chapter 2 of the manual, and the reasoning behind rows 1 and 10 of the resilience assessment (Chapter 7).

Farid Haddad (fictional), the receptionist, receives an e-mail with an attachment named invoice.pdf.exe and opens it on his laboratory workstation. The program runs under the account f.haddad. In many small offices, every employee is a member of every group "to avoid support calls", and every employee is a local administrator. NorthMaple compares that configuration with the role table of LAB_02: in the first case the program reaches five folders out of five, including the client records and the system files; in the second case it reaches only the front-desk folder. The comparison is done on paper with the script below — no malicious program is ever executed, in the laboratory or elsewhere.

Deliverable of this example: The two printed counts (5/5 and 1/5) and the conclusion line, as the justification of the least-privilege memberships in Chapter 2.

Illustration script — nm_least_privilege_reach.py (Python 3)

Task: The script lists the folders of the file server with the one group that needs each folder, defines two configurations of the same company, and counts how many folders a program started by the receptionist account can reach in each configuration.

Relation to the lecture: It quantifies least privilege and need-to-know: the reach of an account (and of any program it starts) equals the set of objects whose groups contain that account.

ready
# The folders of NorthMaple Accounting Inc. on the file server, each with the ONE group that needs it (need-to-know: one folder, one role).FOLDERS = {    "ClientRecords": "accountants",    "TechDocs":      "technicians",    "FrontDesk":     "reception",    "ITAdmin":       "itadmins",    "SystemFiles":   "itadmins",} # Two configurations of the same company: the common mistake (every user in every group) and the least-privilege role table of LAB_02.POLICIES = {    "Everyone is admin": {"f.haddad": ["accountants", "technicians", "reception", "itadmins"]},    "Least privilege":   {"f.haddad": ["reception"]},} # The account that opened the phishing attachment: a program always runs with the rights of the account that started it.INFECTED_USER = "f.haddad" # A function that answers one question: can an account with these groups reach this folder? Yes when the folder's group is one of them.def can_reach(groups_of_user, folder):    # The folder is reachable when its group appears in the group list of the account.    return FOLDERS[folder] in groups_of_user # Evaluate the two configurations one after the other, so that the difference is visible in the output.for policy_name, members in POLICIES.items():    # The groups of the infected account under this configuration.    groups = members[INFECTED_USER]    # The folders the program can reach = the folders whose group contains the infected account.    reachable = [f for f in FOLDERS if can_reach(groups, f)]    # Print the count for this configuration: how many folders out of the total are exposed by this single infected account.    print(f"{policy_name}: a program running as '{INFECTED_USER}' reaches {len(reachable)}/{len(FOLDERS)} folders -> {reachable}") # Print the conclusion the students must keep: the size of the permission set decides the size of the damage.print("Conclusion: the smaller the permission set of an account, the smaller the damage one infected account can cause.")

Step-by-step explanation

  1. FOLDERS maps each folder of the file server to the single group that needs it — the need-to-know decision written down.
  2. POLICIES holds two configurations of the same company. In the first, the receptionist is a member of all four groups; in the second, of the reception group only.
  3. INFECTED_USER is the account that started the program; the script never runs a program, it only computes what that account can reach.
  4. can_reach() is the whole access control decision in one line: the folder is reachable when its group is in the account's group list.
  5. The for loop applies the decision to every folder under each configuration and prints the count (5/5, then 1/5).
  6. The last print states the conclusion that is copied into the manual as the justification of the least-privilege memberships.
  7. In the laboratory the same test is made for real, without any malware, with the LAB_02 validation checklist: log in as f.haddad and try to open each folder.

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

State the principle of least privilege.
Every identity holds only the permissions and privileges strictly required for its assigned task, for the shortest time required, and nothing more.
How do least privilege and need-to-know differ?
Least privilege limits the level of access (NONE, READ, USE, ADMIN); need-to-know limits the scope of information (which data) inside a given level.
What is privilege creep, and what corrects it?
The accumulation of permissions that were never removed after they stopped being needed. It is corrected by periodic access reviews that remove unused rights.
With which rights does a program started by a user run?
With the permissions and privileges of the account that started it — it obtains more only by exploiting a vulnerability.
Why must daily work never use an administrative account?
Every program launched during daily work, including a malicious attachment, would hold administrative rights; a separate administrative account, used only for the task, keeps those rights out of reach.

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. Which situation violates the principle of least privilege?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Look for a right granted beyond what the task needs.

✗ An accountant holds USE on the ClientRecords folder. — USE on the data of the role is exactly what the task requires.

✓ The receptionist is placed in the Administrators group so that a printer can be installed once. — Correct: a permanent, system-wide privilege is granted for a one-time task; the administrator should install the printer with the administrative account.

✗ The IT administrator uses a separate account for daily e-mail and documents. — This is an application of least privilege: privileges stay in the administrative account only.

✗ Technicians may run only the update commands with sudo. — A restricted sudo rule is least privilege applied to administration.

Q2. Which case is an application of need-to-know?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Need-to-know works inside one privilege level and concerns the scope of information.

✓ Two accountants with the same privilege level see different client folders, according to the clients assigned to them. — Correct: same level (USE), different scope of information.

✗ All users receive READ on every folder to simplify support. — This is the opposite: information is exposed to roles that do not need it.

✗ The administrator disables the account of an employee who left. — That is the leaver step of the identity life cycle (section 1.4).

✗ The firewall blocks an incoming port. — That is perimeter filtering (LAB_05), not information scope.

Q3. What is the name of the accumulation of permissions over time when old rights are never removed?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The word describes a slow, unnoticed growth, not an attack.

✗ Privilege escalation. — Privilege escalation is an attacker obtaining higher rights by exploiting a weakness; it is an attack, not an administrative omission.

✓ Privilege creep. — Correct: rights accumulate because nobody removes them when roles change.

✗ Separation of duties. — Separation of duties divides a sensitive operation between several identities.

✗ Inheritance. — Inheritance is the propagation of permissions from a folder to its content (Class 4).

Q4. In the example, why does the program started by f.haddad reach only the FrontDesk folder under the role table?one answer — 4 options

Hint: A program has the groups of the account that started it.

✗ Because the antivirus blocked it. — No antivirus is involved in the computation; the reach is decided by permissions alone.

✓ Because the program holds the group memberships of f.haddad, and those grant access to the reception folder only. — Correct: the program's reach equals the set of folders whose groups contain the account.

✗ Because the file server was switched off. — The server is available in both configurations; only the memberships differ.

✗ Because the other folders are encrypted. — Encryption of stored data is LAB_06; here the difference comes only from the group memberships.

Q5. Which measures implement least privilege? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Look for measures that reduce rights to what the task needs.

✓ A separate administrative account for the IT administrator. — Privileges stay in the account used only for administrative tasks.

✓ A sudo rule limited to the update commands for technicians. — Administration restricted to the commands the role needs.

✗ Giving every user Modify on every folder to reduce support calls. — This grants far more than the tasks need.

✓ Removing the old role group when an employee changes role. — Removal of rights that are no longer needed.

✓ Starting each role at NONE and adding only what is justified. — The construction method of the access matrix.

✗ Sharing one administrator password among the technicians. — A shared account removes accountability and gives full privileges to every holder of the password.

Q6. Which rows of the resilience assessment template (Chapter 7) are directly reduced by least privilege? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Least privilege limits what a compromised account or service can reach.

✓ Row 1 — a phishing e-mail plants malware on one user workstation. — The malware runs with the user's rights; least privilege limits its reach.

✓ Row 3 — the public web server in the DMZ is compromised. — A web service running under a low-privilege account limits what the attacker obtains on that server.

✗ Row 6 — a remote worker's traffic is intercepted on public Wi-Fi. — Interception is countered by encryption in transit (VPN (Virtual Private Network), LAB_06), not by permissions.

✗ Row 7 — a DoS attempt targets the public service. — Availability attacks are countered by firewall and service configuration, not by permissions.

✓ Row 8 — an accountant tries to open the technicians' and administrator's data. — This is exactly what need-to-know and least privilege deny.

✓ Row 10 — ransomware attempts to encrypt the file server. — Ransomware can encrypt only what the compromised account can write to.

1.3 Digital identities, permissions, and access: users, groups, and roles on Windows and Linux 10 min

Slides 15–18 of the deck — 15 1.3 Identities on Windows and Linux (1/2); 16 1.3 Windows and Linux, side by side (2/2); 17 1.3 The identity model of the course; 18 1.3 Example and scripts — nm_identities.sh / nm_identities.ps1
Slide 15Slide 16Slide 17Slide 18

An identity on an operating system is a record with a name, a unique numeric identifier, a home folder (or a profile), a login shell (or a logon method), and security attributes. Two families of identities exist on every machine of the NorthMaple laboratory: user accounts for people, and service accounts for programs (the web server runs as www-data on Linux and as an application-pool identity on Windows). Least privilege applies to both families.

Windows

  • A local account is stored in the SAM (Security Account Manager) database of one machine; a domain account is stored in Active Directory and is valid on every machine of the domain (Class 4). LAB_02 uses local accounts.
  • Every account and every group carries a SID (Security Identifier), for example S-1-5-21-…-1001. Permissions are stored with SIDs, not with names: renaming an account changes nothing in the permissions, and deleting then re-creating an account with the same name produces a new SID that matches no existing permission.
  • Built-in groups with a fixed meaning: Administrators (full control of the machine), Users (ordinary work), Guests, Remote Desktop Users, Backup Operators. Role groups of the company (Accountants, Technicians, Reception, ITAdmins) are created in addition, and users are placed in them.
  • Tools: Computer Management (lusrmgr.msc), the commands net user and net localgroup, and the PowerShell module Microsoft.PowerShell.LocalAccounts: New-LocalUser, New-LocalGroup, Add-LocalGroupMember, Get-LocalGroupMember (Microsoft Learn — LocalAccounts module).

Linux

  • Accounts are records in /etc/passwd (name, UID (User Identifier), primary GID (Group Identifier), home folder, login shell); password hashes are in /etc/shadow, readable by root only; groups and their member lists are in /etc/group.
  • UID 0 is root, the account that bypasses permission checks. System accounts for services use UIDs below 1000; people receive UIDs from 1000 upward. Each user has one primary group and any number of supplementary groups.
  • The administrative group differs by distribution: sudo on Debian and Ubuntu, wheel on Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux. Membership of that group is the Linux equivalent of the Windows Administrators group.
  • Tools: useradd, usermod, userdel, groupadd, gpasswd, passwd, chage, and the query commands id and getent. Debian and Ubuntu also ship the interactive adduser. Reference: man7.org — useradd(8).

Roles and groups — the rule of this course

A role is a business function (Accountant); a group is the technical object that implements it. The rule applied in every lab: permissions are assigned to groups only, never to individual accounts; accounts are placed in groups; there is one group per role. The benefit is measurable at the access review: to see who can modify the client records, one command lists the members of one group. Naming convention of the laboratory: accounts as first-initial.lastname (a.tremblay), groups as lowercase plural nouns, and the description field of the account carries the full name and the role.

ConceptWindows (local machine)Linux
Identity storeSAM database/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow
Unique identifierSIDUID (and GID for groups)
Highest-privilege identityBuilt-in Administrator, group Administratorsroot (UID 0), group sudo / wheel
Ordinary usersGroup UsersUID ≥ 1000, primary group of the same name
Create a userNew-LocalUser, net user /adduseradd -m, adduser
Create a groupNew-LocalGroup, net localgroup /addgroupadd
Add a memberAdd-LocalGroupMemberusermod -aG, gpasswd -a
List membersGet-LocalGroupMembergetent group, id
Force a password change at next logonnet user name /logonpasswordchg:yeschage -d 0 name

Real-life example — Create the identities and role groups of NorthMaple on the Linux file server

Task: Create the four role groups and the seven staff accounts of the company on the Linux machine of the laboratory, place every account in the group of its role, give the administrator controlled root access through the sudo group, and export the memberships as evidence.

Relation to the lecture: The script implements step (3) of privilege and access management: the identities and groups that carry the decision of the access matrix. The same operations, written in PowerShell for the Windows workstation, are provided as a second script.

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: This is LAB_02 part 1 (users and groups on one Windows machine and one Linux machine, following the role table). The output of getent is the membership evidence of Chapter 2 of the manual. The remote worker of the role table is one of the accountants (Chloé Roy works from home) and receives the VPN (Virtual Private Network) group in LAB_06.

The company has seven staff members (all fictional): three accountants (Alice Tremblay, Bob Nguyen, Chloé Roy), two technicians (David Kim, Emma Bouchard), one receptionist (Farid Haddad) and one IT administrator (Gina Lopez). Gina creates one group per role, one account per person, and places each account in exactly one role group. Nobody works as root: Gina's own account joins the sudo group. Every account receives a laboratory-only initial password that must be changed at the first login. The last loop prints the members of every role group — that output is the screenshot for the manual.

Deliverable of this example: Screenshot of the four getent lines (group memberships) and of the id output for one account of each role — Chapter 2, section N.3 and N.4 of the manual.

Illustration script — nm_identities.sh (Bash (Linux))

Task: The script creates the role groups and the staff accounts of NorthMaple on a Debian or Ubuntu machine, assigns memberships, sets laboratory-only initial passwords with a forced change, and prints the membership evidence.

Relation to the lecture: It is the technical implementation of RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) on Linux: one group per role, users placed in groups, permissions (Class 4) later attached to the groups only.

ready
#!/usr/bin/env bash# Stop the script at the first failing command, so that a half-created set of identities is never left behind.set -e # Create one group per role. The group is the object that will receive the folder permissions in Class 4; users only join groups.sudo groupadd accountantssudo groupadd technicianssudo groupadd receptionsudo groupadd itadmins # Create the staff accounts (fictional people). -m creates the home folder, -c stores the full name and role, -s sets the login shell.sudo useradd -m -c "Alice Tremblay - Accountant" -s /bin/bash a.tremblaysudo useradd -m -c "Bob Nguyen - Accountant" -s /bin/bash b.nguyensudo useradd -m -c "Chloe Roy - Accountant (remote worker)" -s /bin/bash c.roysudo useradd -m -c "David Kim - Technician" -s /bin/bash d.kimsudo useradd -m -c "Emma Bouchard - Technician" -s /bin/bash e.bouchardsudo useradd -m -c "Farid Haddad - Receptionist" -s /bin/bash f.haddadsudo useradd -m -c "Gina Lopez - IT Administrator" -s /bin/bash g.lopez # Place each account in the group of its role. -aG appends a supplementary group; without -a, the existing memberships would be replaced.sudo usermod -aG accountants a.tremblaysudo usermod -aG accountants b.nguyensudo usermod -aG accountants c.roysudo usermod -aG technicians d.kimsudo usermod -aG technicians e.bouchardsudo usermod -aG reception f.haddadsudo usermod -aG itadmins g.lopez # Give the administrator controlled root access through the sudo group (on Fedora or Red Hat the group is named wheel).sudo usermod -aG sudo g.lopez # Set a laboratory-only initial password for every account, then force a change at the first login (chage -d 0 expires the password now).for u in a.tremblay b.nguyen c.roy d.kim e.bouchard f.haddad g.lopez; do  echo "$u:Lab-Only-Initial-2026!" | sudo chpasswd  sudo chage -d 0 "$u"done # Evidence for the manual: print the member list of every role group (the fourth field of the group record).for g in accountants technicians reception itadmins sudo; do  echo "$g: $(getent group "$g" | cut -d: -f4)"done

Step-by-step explanation

  1. set -e makes the shell stop at the first error, so that a typo cannot leave three groups created and four missing.
  2. The four groupadd commands create the role groups. Groups come first because the accounts are placed in them immediately after.
  3. Each useradd -m -c … -s /bin/bash name creates one account with a home folder, a description (full name and role) and a login shell.
  4. Each usermod -aG group user appends one supplementary group to the account. The -a option is essential: without it, -G replaces the list of supplementary groups.
  5. usermod -aG sudo g.lopez gives the administrator the right to run commands as root with sudo, after typing her own password (Class 4).
  6. The first loop sets the same laboratory-only initial password on every account with chpasswd, then chage -d 0 expires it immediately so that each person chooses a personal password at the first login. Laboratory-only passwords never leave the isolated environment.
  7. The last loop prints, for every group, the fourth field of the getent group record — the comma-separated member list. That output is the evidence screenshot.
  8. To run it: save the file, chmod +x nm_identities.sh, then ./nm_identities.sh on the Linux machine of the laboratory. The Windows counterpart nm_identities.ps1 performs the same steps with the LocalAccounts module.

Counterpart — nm_identities.ps1 (PowerShell, Windows)

The same identities on the Windows workstation of the laboratory (run in an elevated PowerShell session). This is the second half of LAB_02 part 1.

# Stop at the first error so that the set of identities is created completely or not at all.
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
# Create one local group per role (the group receives the NTFS permissions in Class 4).
foreach ($g in "Accountants","Technicians","Reception","ITAdmins") { New-LocalGroup -Name $g -Description "NorthMaple role group" }
# The staff list: account name, full name, role group. All people are fictional.
$staff = @(
  @{Name="a.tremblay"; Full="Alice Tremblay - Accountant";               Group="Accountants"},
  @{Name="b.nguyen";   Full="Bob Nguyen - Accountant";                   Group="Accountants"},
  @{Name="c.roy";      Full="Chloe Roy - Accountant (remote worker)";    Group="Accountants"},
  @{Name="d.kim";      Full="David Kim - Technician";                    Group="Technicians"},
  @{Name="e.bouchard"; Full="Emma Bouchard - Technician";                Group="Technicians"},
  @{Name="f.haddad";   Full="Farid Haddad - Receptionist";               Group="Reception"},
  @{Name="g.lopez";    Full="Gina Lopez - IT Administrator";             Group="ITAdmins"}
)
# Laboratory-only initial password, converted to the secure format the command requires.
$initial = ConvertTo-SecureString "Lab-Only-Initial-2026!" -AsPlainText -Force
# Create each account, force a password change at the first logon, and place it in its role group.
foreach ($s in $staff) {
  New-LocalUser -Name $s.Name -FullName $s.Full -Password $initial -PasswordNeverExpires:$false | Out-Null
  net user $s.Name /logonpasswordchg:yes | Out-Null
  Add-LocalGroupMember -Group $s.Group -Member $s.Name
}
# Technicians hold limited administrative rights on the workstation only: local Administrators on this machine, nowhere else.
Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "Technicians"
# The IT administrator administers through a separate account (created in Class 4, section 2.3), not through the daily account.
# Evidence for the manual: the members of every role group.
foreach ($g in "Accountants","Technicians","Reception","ITAdmins","Administrators") { "$g : " + ((Get-LocalGroupMember -Group $g).Name -join ", ") }

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

Where does Linux store accounts, password hashes, and groups?
Accounts in /etc/passwd, password hashes in /etc/shadow (readable by root only), groups and member lists in /etc/group.
What identifies an account in a Windows permission entry?
Its SID (Security Identifier) (Security Identifier), never its name. Renaming changes nothing; deleting and re-creating produces a new SID that matches no permission.
What is the difference between a role and a group?
A role is a business function (Accountant); a group is the technical object that implements the role and receives the permissions.
Why is the -a option required in usermod -aG group user?
-a appends the group to the account's supplementary groups; without it, -G replaces the whole list and removes the existing memberships.
Which identities hold the highest privilege on each system, and what is the rule about them?
root (UID (User Identifier) 0) and the sudo/wheel group on Linux; the built-in Administrator and the Administrators group on Windows. They are never used for daily work.

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. Which file stores the password hashes on a Linux system?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The file is readable by root only.

✗ /etc/passwd — /etc/passwd holds the account records (name, UID, GID (Group Identifier), home, shell); the password field contains only a placeholder.

✓ /etc/shadow — Correct: /etc/shadow holds the hashes and the password-ageing information, readable by root only.

✗ /etc/group — /etc/group holds the groups and their member lists.

✗ /etc/sudoers — /etc/sudoers holds the sudo rules (Class 4).

Q2. An administrator renames the Windows account a.tremblay to alice.tremblay. What happens to the permissions of that account?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Permission entries store an identifier, not a name.

✗ They are lost and must be granted again. — Nothing is lost: the entries reference the SID, which does not change.

✓ They stay unchanged, because the entries store the SID. — Correct: the SID is the identity in every permission entry; the display name is only resolved for reading.

✗ They are duplicated under both names. — There is only one account and one SID.

✗ They are transferred to the Users group. — Group membership is not affected by a rename.

Q3. Which command adds d.kim to the technicians group without removing the other memberships of the account?one answer — 4 options

Hint: One option appends, one replaces.

✗ usermod -G technicians d.kim — Without -a, -G replaces the list of supplementary groups: the other memberships are removed.

✓ usermod -aG technicians d.kim — Correct: -a appends technicians to the existing supplementary groups.

✗ groupadd d.kim — groupadd creates a group named d.kim; it does not change memberships.

✗ useradd technicians — useradd creates a new user account named technicians.

Q4. What is the rule of this course for assigning permissions?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The rule makes the access review a one-command operation.

✗ Assign permissions to each user account individually. — Individual assignments cannot be reviewed efficiently and lead to privilege creep.

✓ Assign permissions to groups only; users receive access by joining the group of their role. — Correct: one group per role, permissions on the group, memberships as the only variable.

✗ Assign all permissions to root or to the Administrators group. — That would force every user to work with administrative privileges.

✗ Assign permissions to Everyone and rely on the firewall. — The firewall is a different layer; Everyone removes the access control layer entirely.

Q5. Which of the following are built-in Windows local groups? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Built-in groups exist on every Windows machine before any group is created by the administrator.

✓ Administrators — Built-in: full control of the machine.

✓ Users — Built-in: ordinary work.

✓ Guests — Built-in: limited, usually disabled.

✗ Accountants — A role group created by NorthMaple, not a built-in group.

✓ Backup Operators — Built-in: may back up and restore files regardless of permissions.

✗ wheel — wheel is the administrative group of Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux, not a Windows group.

Q6. Which fields are part of a record in /etc/passwd? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Seven fields separated by colons; two kinds of information live in other files.

✓ The account name. — First field.

✓ The UID. — Third field.

✓ The home folder. — Sixth field.

✓ The login shell. — Seventh field.

✗ The password hash. — The hash is in /etc/shadow; /etc/passwd holds only a placeholder character.

✗ The list of supplementary groups. — Supplementary memberships are in /etc/group; /etc/passwd holds only the primary GID.

1.4 Overview of the processes and tools used to grant, review, and remove access 8 min

Slides 19–22 of the deck — 19 1.4 The identity life cycle (1/2); 20 1.4 The access review (2/2); 21 1.4 Joiner, mover, leaver — and the review loop; 22 1.4 Example — nm_access_review.py
Slide 19Slide 20Slide 21Slide 22

Access is not configured once; it follows an identity life cycle with three events and one recurring control. Each event is a documented procedure with a request, an approval, an action, and a record.

  1. Joiner (onboarding). The HR (Human Resources) department confirms the person and the role; the owner of the resource approves the request; the administrator creates the identity, places it in the role group, sets a temporary password that must be changed at the first login, and records the action: date, requester, approver, evidence (the membership export).
  2. Mover (role change). The old role group is removed before the new one is added. Rights left behind at role changes are the main source of privilege creep.
  3. Leaver (offboarding). On the last day, the account is disabled, not deleted: its files must remain attributable and its audit history must remain readable. Remote access (VPN (Virtual Private Network), SSH (Secure Shell) keys) is revoked, every shared secret the person knew is changed, and the account is deleted only after the retention period defined by the company.

The recurring control is the access review (also called recertification): at fixed intervals (quarterly for user accounts, monthly for administrative accounts), the owner of each resource compares the actual group memberships with the role table and confirms or revokes each entry. A review without evidence is not a review; the evidence set contains the membership exports (getent group, Get-LocalGroupMember), the last-logon dates, the list of accounts with administrative rights, and the list of disabled accounts. Accounts without activity for 45 days are disabled — this is requirement 5.3 of CIS (Center for Internet Security) Control 5 (cisecurity.org — Control 5); Control 6 requires a documented process for granting and revoking access (cisecurity.org — Control 6).

Tools, by size of organization. At the size of NorthMaple and of the laboratory: command-line exports and a spreadsheet (the review template of this section), with approvals kept as e-mails or signed forms. In larger organizations: a directory service (Active Directory, FreeIPA), an IAM (Identity and Access Management) platform that automates joiner-mover-leaver from the HR system, and a ticketing system that stores requests and approvals. Open-source directory and identity products, at awareness level: FreeIPA and Keycloak.

What the Course Procedure Manual must state for Chapter 2: who may approve an access request (the owner of the data), which evidence is kept for each event, and the review calendar. A procedure that a colleague can reproduce contains these three elements and the exact commands used.

EventTriggerAction on the systemsRecord kept
JoinerHR confirms hire and roleCreate account; add to the role group; temporary password with forced changeRequest, approval, membership export, date
MoverHR confirms role changeRemove old role group; add new role group; review remaining rightsBefore/after membership export
LeaverHR confirms last dayDisable account; revoke VPN and keys; rotate shared secrets; delete after retentionDisable confirmation, revocation list, date
Access reviewCalendar (quarterly; monthly for admins)Compare memberships with the role table; remove unused rights; disable dormant accountsSigned review sheet with evidence

Real-life example — Run the first quarterly access review of NorthMaple

Task: Compare the role table confirmed by HR with the accounts and memberships found on the Linux server, and produce the list of corrective actions: create, grant, remove, disable.

Relation to the lecture: This is step (4) of privilege and access management — the review — and it produces the actions of steps (3) and (5): grant and remove. Each finding corresponds to one event of the life cycle.

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: The corrective actions are applied with the commands of section 1.3; the review sheet is the evidence of Chapter 2 (validation, section N.4 of the manual) and the entry of section N.5 (problems met and fixes). The review template is one of the downloadable files of this lecture.

Three months after the creation of the accounts, HR confirms four changes: Farid Haddad left the company; Emma Bouchard moved from technician to receptionist to replace him; Harpreet Singh (fictional) joined as technician; and the server still carries an old service account, svc-backup-old, that nobody owns. Gina exports the memberships with getent, compares them with the HR list, and obtains five actions: disable f.haddad, remove e.bouchard from technicians then add her to reception, create h.singh in technicians, and disable the orphan service account pending investigation. Three accounts are confirmed unchanged.

Deliverable of this example: The review sheet (access_review_template.csv filled in), the list of actions with their dates, and the before/after membership exports — Chapter 2 of the manual.

Illustration script — nm_access_review.py (Python 3)

Task: The script compares the HR role table (the authoritative source) with the state of the accounts on the server and prints one corrective action per difference: CREATE, GRANT, REMOVE, DISABLE, or OK.

Relation to the lecture: It automates the access review: privilege creep, leavers still enabled, joiners without accounts and orphan accounts are detected by comparing two lists, not by memory.

ready
# The HR view: the authoritative list of who works at NorthMaple today, with the role and the employment status of each person.HR = {    "a.tremblay": ("Accountant",         "active"),    "b.nguyen":   ("Accountant",         "active"),    "c.roy":      ("Accountant",         "active"),    "d.kim":      ("Technician",         "active"),    "e.bouchard": ("Receptionist",       "active"),   # mover: was a technician last quarter    "f.haddad":   ("Receptionist",       "left"),     # leaver: left the company    "g.lopez":    ("Administrator (IT)", "active"),    "h.singh":    ("Technician",         "active"),   # joiner: hired this quarter} # The group that implements each role, and the extra group that only the IT administrator may hold.ROLE_GROUP = {"Accountant": "accountants", "Technician": "technicians", "Receptionist": "reception", "Administrator (IT)": "itadmins"} # The system view: what the server reports today (collected with getent group and passwd -S before the review).SYSTEM = {    "a.tremblay":     {"enabled": True, "groups": {"accountants"}},    "b.nguyen":       {"enabled": True, "groups": {"accountants"}},    "c.roy":          {"enabled": True, "groups": {"accountants"}},    "d.kim":          {"enabled": True, "groups": {"technicians"}},    "e.bouchard":     {"enabled": True, "groups": {"technicians"}},   # still in the old role group: privilege creep    "f.haddad":       {"enabled": True, "groups": {"reception"}},     # still enabled although the person left    "g.lopez":        {"enabled": True, "groups": {"itadmins", "sudo"}},    "svc-backup-old": {"enabled": True, "groups": {"itadmins"}},      # nobody in HR owns this account} # The list that will receive one corrective action per finding.actions = [] # Walk through the HR list: every person known to HR must have exactly the memberships of the role, and leavers must be disabled.for user, (role, status) in HR.items():    # A person who left must have a disabled account, whatever the groups are.    if status == "left":        actions.append((user, "DISABLE", "leaver: the person no longer works here"))        continue    # A person without an account is a joiner: the account must be created and placed in the role group.    if user not in SYSTEM:        actions.append((user, "CREATE + GRANT " + ROLE_GROUP[role], "joiner: no account exists yet"))        continue    # The set of groups the role requires: the role group, plus sudo for the IT administrator only.    expected = {ROLE_GROUP[role]} | ({"sudo"} if role == "Administrator (IT)" else set())    # The groups the account actually holds on the server.    found = SYSTEM[user]["groups"]    # Missing memberships are granted; memberships beyond the role are removed (this is where privilege creep is corrected).    for g in sorted(expected - found):        actions.append((user, "GRANT " + g, "the role requires this group"))    for g in sorted(found - expected):        actions.append((user, "REMOVE " + g, "the role does not require this group"))    # An account with exactly the expected groups is confirmed.    if expected == found:        actions.append((user, "OK", "memberships match the role table")) # Accounts that exist on the server but are unknown to HR are orphan accounts: they are disabled and investigated.for user in SYSTEM:    if user not in HR:        actions.append((user, "DISABLE", "orphan account: no owner in the HR list - investigate")) # Print the review sheet: one line per finding, ready to be pasted into the access-review template.for user, action, reason in actions:    print(f"{user:16} {action:24} {reason}")

Step-by-step explanation

  1. HR is the authoritative source: the review always compares the systems against HR, never the reverse.
  2. ROLE_GROUP translates each business role into the group that implements it — the same translation as in section 1.3.
  3. SYSTEM is the state exported from the server before the review (in the laboratory: the output of getent group and passwd -S).
  4. The first loop handles every person in HR: leavers are disabled; joiners without an account are created and granted; for everybody else the script computes the expected groups and compares them with the groups found.
  5. The set operations expected - found and found - expected give the grants and the removals; a removal is exactly the correction of privilege creep.
  6. The second loop finds accounts that exist on the server without an owner in HR — orphan accounts are disabled and investigated.
  7. The final loop prints the review sheet; each line becomes one row of the access-review template, with the date and the name of the reviewer added.
  8. The corrective actions are then applied with the commands of section 1.3 (usermod -aG, gpasswd -d, usermod -L to lock an account), and a second export proves the result.

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

Name the three events of the identity life cycle.
Joiner (onboarding), mover (role change), leaver (offboarding).
Why is an account disabled, not deleted, on the last day?
So that the files stay attributable and the audit history stays readable; the account is deleted after the retention period.
What is an access review?
A periodic comparison, by the owner of each resource, of the actual memberships with the role table, with evidence, ending with the confirmation or the revocation of each entry.
What is the rule for a mover?
Remove the old role group before adding the new one, then review the remaining rights.
After how many days of inactivity does CIS Control 5 require an account to be disabled?
45 days.

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. What is the first action on the last working day of an employee?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Files and audit history must remain readable.

✗ Delete the account immediately. — Deleting removes the attribution of the files and complicates the audit; the account is deleted after the retention period.

✓ Disable the account and revoke the remote access. — Correct: disable, revoke VPN (Virtual Private Network) and keys, rotate the secrets the person knew, delete later.

✗ Move the account to the Guests group. — A group change leaves the account usable.

✗ Do nothing until the next quarterly review. — A leaver with an enabled account is an open entry point for up to three months.

Q2. What is the main source of privilege creep?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Look at the mover event.

✗ New hires receiving too many groups. — Joiners start from the role group; the problem is rather what is not removed later.

✓ Role changes where the old rights are never removed. — Correct: movers keep the old role group in addition to the new one.

✗ Too many role groups in the company. — The number of groups does not by itself grant rights.

✗ Strong password policies. — Passwords concern authentication, not the accumulation of permissions.

Q3. During an access review, who confirms that a membership is still needed?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The decision belongs to the person responsible for the data.

✗ The user who holds the membership. — The user is not the owner of the resource and would keep every right.

✓ The owner of the resource or of the data. — Correct: the owner knows which roles need the data and signs the review.

✗ The antivirus software. — Antivirus software does not evaluate business needs.

✗ The administrator of the firewall. — The firewall administrator manages a different layer.

Q4. Which command output is valid evidence of memberships for a review on Linux?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The evidence must show who is in which group.

✗ ls -l /home — It lists home folders and their owners, not group memberships.

✓ getent group accountants — Correct: it prints the group record with its member list.

✗ ping fileserver — It tests network reachability, not access.

✗ df -h — It shows disk usage.

Q5. Which actions are part of a complete offboarding? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Everything the person could still use to come back must be closed.

✓ Disable the account. — First action of the leaver procedure.

✓ Revoke the VPN access and the SSH keys. — Remote access is a separate path that must be closed explicitly.

✓ Change every shared secret the person knew. — Shared passwords known by a leaver are no longer secret.

✓ Record the action with the date and the approver. — Every event ends with a record.

✗ Grant READ on everything for one month as a transition. — This extends the access of a person who no longer works there.

✗ Send the password of the account to the manager. — Passwords are never transmitted; the manager obtains the files through a documented procedure.

Q6. Which items belong in the evidence set of an access review? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Evidence shows the state of the accounts, never secrets.

✓ The export of the group memberships. — The core evidence: who is in which group.

✓ The list of accounts with administrative rights. — Administrative accounts are reviewed monthly.

✓ The last-logon dates. — They reveal dormant accounts (45-day rule).

✓ The list of disabled accounts. — It proves that leavers were processed.

✗ The passwords of the users. — Passwords are never exported; the review concerns authorization, not secrets.

✗ The firewall rule set. — The firewall rule set is the evidence of LAB_05, a different layer.

Lesson 1 — checkpoint

Five sentences to remember

  1. Every access control decision has a subject, an operation and an object.
  2. A permission belongs to the object; a privilege belongs to the identity.
  3. Least privilege limits the level of access; need-to-know limits its scope.
  4. One group per role; permissions are attached to groups only.
  5. Joiner, mover, leaver; review with evidence; disable before delete.

Network Access Control and Security — part 2 — LAB_02 introduction

Lesson 2 covers the mechanisms: how Windows enforces the decisions with NTFS (New Technology File System) permissions, shares and Active Directory (2.1), how Linux enforces them with ownership, permission bits and sudo (2.2), the techniques that secure access to sensitive data and systems (2.3), and the malware families that abuse weak access control, with basic detection and prevention (2.4). The lesson ends with the introduction of LAB_02.

2.1 Windows access control: NTFS (New Technology File System) permissions, sharing, and an introduction to Active Directory 12 min

Slides 25–29 of the deck — 25 2.1 NTFS permissions (1/3); 26 2.1 The five evaluation rules and sharing (2/3); 27 2.1 Active Directory at awareness level (3/3); 28 2.1 How Windows decides; 29 2.1 Example — Set-NorthMapleNtfs.ps1
Slide 25Slide 26Slide 27Slide 28Slide 29

NTFS (New Technology File System) stores, together with every file and folder, a security descriptor. The descriptor contains the SID (Security Identifier) of the owner, a DACL (Discretionary Access Control List) that lists who may do what, and a SACL (System Access Control List) that lists which access attempts must be recorded in the security log (section 2.3). Each entry of a list is an ACE (Access Control Entry): a SID (a user or, in this course, always a group), an access type (Allow or Deny), a set of rights, and inheritance flags. The ACL (Access Control List) is the list itself; the commands of this section read and write it. Reference: Microsoft Learn — Access Control Lists.

The six basic permissions (each one is a bundle of advanced rights): Full control, Modify, Read & execute, List folder contents (folders only), Read, Write. Modify = read + write + execute + delete, without the right to change permissions or to take ownership; those two rights belong to Full control only. The role groups of NorthMaple receive Modify on their own folder; Full control stays with Administrators and with the SYSTEM account.

The five evaluation rules applied by the system when an identity opens an object:

  1. Permissions are cumulative across all the groups of the identity: a member of Accountants (Modify) and of Users (Read) obtains Modify.
  2. An explicit Deny entry overrides any Allow entry, from any group.
  3. An explicit entry (set on the object) overrides an inherited entry (received from the parent folder).
  4. An identity that appears in no entry receives no access at all — the implicit deny.
  5. Inheritance: entries flow from a folder to its files and sub-folders unless inheritance is disabled on the child. In the icacls notation, (OI) means "object inherit" (files) and (CI) "container inherit" (sub-folders).

The owner can always change the DACL of its objects; a member of Administrators can take ownership of any object — a privilege (user right), which is why Administrators membership is reserved.

Sharing. A folder published on the network through the SMB (Server Message Block) protocol carries a second, independent list: the share permissions (Full control, Change, Read). For an access that comes through the network, the effective access is the more restrictive of the share permissions and of the NTFS permissions. The practice of this course: share permissions give Change to the role group and Full control to Administrators; the fine decisions are made in NTFS, where they apply both locally and through the network.

Tools. File Explorer → Properties → Security (graphical); icacls on the command line (Microsoft Learn — icacls); PowerShell Get-Acl, Set-Acl, New-SmbShare, Get-SmbShareAccess. The elevation prompt of UAC (User Account Control) appears each time an administrative account changes an ACL — that prompt is the Windows form of "elevate for the task only".

Active Directory, at awareness level

  • AD DS (Active Directory Domain Services) is a central directory database hosted on one or more servers called DC (Domain Controller). Accounts and groups stored there are domain accounts and domain groups, valid on every computer that has joined the domain; the SAM (Security Account Manager) of each computer keeps only its local accounts.
  • Objects (users, groups, computers) are organized in OU (Organizational Unit) containers. A GPO (Group Policy Object) attached to an OU pushes security policies — password length, lockout thresholds, user rights, firewall settings, screen lock — to all the users and computers of that OU.
  • Authentication in a domain uses the Kerberos protocol: the DC issues time-limited tickets, so that a workstation never sees the password of the user in clear text. The recommended group nesting is AGDLP (Accounts, Global groups, Domain Local groups, Permissions): accounts go into global groups (roles), global groups into domain local groups (resource access), and permissions are set on the domain local groups.
  • LAB_02 uses local accounts on standalone machines: no domain controller is required. The design rule is identical — permissions on groups, users in groups — which is why a design made with local groups transfers to a domain without change. Reference: Microsoft Learn — AD DS overview.
