Real-life example — Protect the ClientRecords folder with NTFS and share permissions

Task: Configure D:\NorthMaple\ClientRecords so that Accountants hold Modify, Administrators and SYSTEM hold Full control, every other identity is refused, share the folder on the network with matching share permissions, and display the resulting lists as evidence.

Relation to the lecture: The script writes explicit ACEs after removing inheritance, then adds the share permissions; the evidence shows the five evaluation rules in action (cumulative rights, implicit deny, inheritance flags, share versus NTFS).

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: LAB_02 part 2 — folder permissions on Windows so that each company role reaches only its own data, validated with test logins (the validation checklist). The printed icacls output and the share access list are the screenshots of Chapter 2, section N.4 of the manual. The same design is repeated for TechDocs (Technicians) and FrontDesk (Reception).

The client records of NorthMaple are confidential. Gina creates D:\NorthMaple\ClientRecords on the Windows file server of the laboratory, disables inheritance so that the generic entries of the D: drive (Users: Read) stop applying, and adds three explicit entries: Administrators — Full control, Accountants — Modify, SYSTEM — Full control. She shares the folder as ClientRecords with Change for Accountants and Full control for Administrators. The validation is a test login: a.tremblay creates and deletes a file (allowed), f.haddad receives "Access is denied" (implicit deny), d.kim (technician, local administrator of the workstations but not of the server) receives the same refusal.

Deliverable of this example: Screenshots of icacls D:\NorthMaple\ClientRecords, of Get-SmbShareAccess, and of the three test logins (one allowed, two refused) — Chapter 2 of the manual.

Illustration script — Set-NorthMapleNtfs.ps1 (PowerShell (Windows))

Task: The script creates the client-records folder, removes inheritance, grants three explicit NTFS entries, shares the folder with matching share permissions, and prints both permission lists as evidence.

Relation to the lecture: It applies the NTFS model of the lecture: ACEs on groups, inheritance flags (OI)(CI), Modify for the role and Full control for administration only, and the share-versus-NTFS rule.

ready
# Stop at the first error, so that the folder is never left half-configured (for example shared before its permissions are set).$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop" # The folder that holds the client financial records - the most sensitive data of NorthMaple Accounting Inc.$Folder = "D:\NorthMaple\ClientRecords" # Create the folder if it does not exist yet; -Force also creates the missing parent folders. Out-Null hides the object that New-Item returns.New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Folder -Force | Out-Null # Step 1 - Remove permission inheritance and delete the inherited entries, so that only the explicit entries added below apply.icacls $Folder /inheritance:r # Step 2 - Give the local Administrators group Full control (F); (OI)(CI) makes the entry inherited by the files and the sub-folders.icacls $Folder /grant "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F" # Step 3 - Give the Accountants role group Modify (M): read, write, create and delete files, but not change permissions or take ownership.icacls $Folder /grant "Accountants:(OI)(CI)M" # Step 4 - Give the SYSTEM account Full control, so that backup, antivirus and indexing services keep working on the folder.icacls $Folder /grant "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" # Step 5 - Publish the folder on the network with share permissions that match the design; the effective network access is the more restrictive of share and NTFS.New-SmbShare -Name "ClientRecords" -Path $Folder -FullAccess "Administrators" -ChangeAccess "Accountants" | Out-Null # Step 6 - Evidence: display the NTFS access control list of the folder (the screenshot for the manual).icacls $Folder # Step 7 - Evidence: display the share permissions of the published share.Get-SmbShareAccess -Name "ClientRecords"

Step-by-step explanation

  1. $ErrorActionPreference = "Stop" turns every error into a stop, so that a failing step never lets the next one run on a wrong basis.
  2. New-Item … -Force creates the folder (and D:\NorthMaple if needed); it does nothing if the folder already exists.
  3. icacls $Folder /inheritance:r removes inheritance and deletes the inherited entries; from this point only explicit entries exist on the folder.
  4. The three /grant lines add explicit Allow entries: Administrators and SYSTEM with Full control (F), Accountants with Modify (M). (OI)(CI) makes each entry propagate to files and sub-folders.
  5. New-SmbShare publishes the folder; the share permissions repeat the design (Change for the role, Full control for administration). Through the network, the more restrictive of the two lists applies.
  6. The last two commands print the lists: icacls shows the NTFS entries with their flags; Get-SmbShareAccess shows the share entries. Both outputs are pasted into Chapter 2.
  7. Validation in the laboratory: log in as an accountant and create a file (expected: allowed); log in as the receptionist and open the folder (expected: Access is denied). Both screenshots go to section N.4 of the manual.
  8. Run in an elevated PowerShell session on the Windows machine of the laboratory: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass then .\Set-NorthMapleNtfs.ps1.

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

What is an ACE?
One entry of an access control list: a SID (Security Identifier) (user or group), Allow or Deny, a set of rights, and inheritance flags.
What does Modify allow, and what does it not allow?
Read, write, execute, create and delete; it does not allow changing permissions or taking ownership — those belong to Full control.
Share permissions give Read and NTFS gives Modify. What is the effective access through the network?
Read — the more restrictive of the two lists applies to network access.
What is the effect of an explicit Deny entry?
It overrides any Allow entry, from any group of the identity.
DACL versus SACL: what does each list contain?
The DACL (Discretionary Access Control List) contains the access decisions (Allow/Deny entries); the SACL (System Access Control List) contains the auditing entries (which attempts are recorded).

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. A user is a member of Accountants (Modify) and of Users (Read) on the same folder. What is the effective NTFS permission?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Rule 1: rights accumulate across groups.

✗ Read. — Rights are cumulative: the higher right of another group is not lost.

✓ Modify. — Correct: the union of Modify and Read is Modify.

✗ Full control. — No entry grants Full control.

✗ No access. — The user appears in two Allow entries.

Q2. The same user is also a member of a group Interns that has an explicit Deny Write. Can the user write?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Rule 2.

✗ Yes, because Modify includes Write. — An explicit Deny overrides the Allow entries.

✓ No, the Deny entry overrides the Allow entries. — Correct: Deny wins over Allow, from any group.

✗ Yes, after a UAC prompt. — UAC (User Account Control) elevates privileges; it does not cancel a Deny entry on the folder.

✗ Only for files, not for sub-folders. — The Deny applies wherever its inheritance flags propagate it.

Q3. Which icacls option removes inheritance and deletes the inherited entries on a folder?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The option acts on inheritance and has a single letter argument.

✗ /grant — /grant adds an Allow entry.

✓ /inheritance:r — Correct: r removes inheritance and the inherited entries; d would copy them as explicit entries first.

✗ /deny — /deny adds a Deny entry.

✗ /reset — /reset replaces the ACL (Access Control List) with the default inherited ACL — the opposite of what is wanted here.

Q4. What is a GPO?one answer — 4 options

Hint: It is an Active Directory object, attached to an OU (Organizational Unit).

✗ A firewall rule on the perimeter. — Firewall rules belong to LAB_05.

✓ A set of settings applied by Active Directory to the users and computers of an OU. — Correct: password policy, lockout, user rights, firewall settings and more are distributed through Group Policy Objects.

✗ A permission entry on a file. — A permission entry is an ACE (Access Control Entry).

✗ A network share. — A share is a published folder.

Q5. Which of the following are NTFS basic permissions? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Six basic permissions exist; one of the options is a share permission.

✓ Full control — Basic permission.

✓ Modify — Basic permission.

✓ Read & execute — Basic permission.

✗ Change — Change is a share permission, not an NTFS (New Technology File System) permission.

✓ Write — Basic permission.

✗ Execute-only — There is no basic permission with this name; execution is part of Read & execute.

Q6. Which statements about Active Directory are correct? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Think about where accounts live, how policies are pushed, and what LAB_02 requires.

✓ Domain accounts are stored on the domain controllers. — AD DS (Active Directory Domain Services) is the central store; the SAM (Security Account Manager) keeps only local accounts.

✓ Group Policy Objects distribute security settings to users and computers. — A GPO (Group Policy Object) attached to an OU applies to its members.

✗ A domain controller is required for LAB_02. — LAB_02 uses local accounts on standalone machines.

✓ Organizational Units organize users, groups and computers. — OUs are the containers to which GPOs are attached.

✗ Share permissions are stored in Active Directory. — Share permissions are stored on the file server that publishes the share.

✓ Kerberos is used for authentication in a domain. — The DC (Domain Controller) issues time-limited tickets.

2.2 Linux access control: file ownership, permission bits, and the sudo mechanism 12 min

Slides 30–33 of the deck — 30 2.2 Ownership and permission bits (1/2); 31 2.2 sudo — controlled administrative access (2/2); 32 2.2 Anatomy of ls -l and of the octal mode; 33 2.2 Example — nm_linux_permissions.sh
Slide 30Slide 31Slide 32Slide 33

Every file and folder on Linux carries one owner (a UID (User Identifier)), one group (a GID (Group Identifier)), and a mode made of permission bits for three classes of subjects: the user class (u, the owner), the group class (g), and others (o, every other account). Each class has three bits: r (read, value 4), w (write, value 2), x (execute, value 1). On a folder, x is the right to enter the folder and reach its entries; r alone lists the names without giving access to them.

Reading ls -l. The line drwxrws--- 2 root accountants 4096 Sep 8 18:40 client-records is read as: d = directory; rwx = owner (root) may read, write, enter; rws = group (accountants) may read, write, enter, and the setgid bit is set; --- = others have nothing.

Octal notation. Add the values of the set bits per class: rwx = 7, rw- = 6, r-x = 5, r-- = 4, --- = 0. Common modes: 750 (owner everything, group read and enter, others nothing), 770, 640, 600. A fourth leading digit carries the three special bits: setuid (4) — a program runs with the identity of its owner (example: /usr/bin/passwd, which must write to /etc/shadow); setgid (2) — on a folder, new files inherit the group of the folder instead of the primary group of their creator, which is essential for a team folder; sticky bit (1) — in a shared folder, only the owner of a file may delete it (/tmp). The role folders of NorthMaple use mode 2770.

The evaluation rule. The system tests one class only: if the subject is the owner, the owner bits decide; otherwise, if the subject is a member of the group, the group bits decide; otherwise the others bits decide. There is no cumulation between classes. The root account bypasses the read and write checks (execution still requires at least one x bit). Fine exceptions — one extra user on one folder — are possible with POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) ACLs (setfacl, getfacl), awareness level.

Commands. chown user:group path sets the owner and the group; chgrp sets the group only; chmod 2770 path sets the mode in octal, chmod g+w path in symbolic form; umask defines the default mode of new files; stat, id, and namei -l display ownership and modes. References: man7.org — chmod(1), man7.org — chown(1).

sudo — controlled administrative access

sudo allows an authorized account to run specific commands as another user, normally root, after authenticating with its own password; every use is written to the authentication log (/var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu, the journal on other distributions), which gives the accounting of the AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) model. The rules live in /etc/sudoers and in the drop-in files of /etc/sudoers.d/; they are edited only with visudo, which checks the syntax before saving (a syntax error in this file locks everyone out of sudo). The syntax of a rule is who where=(as_whom) commands:

  • %technicians ALL=(root) /usr/bin/apt update, /usr/bin/apt upgrade — members of the group technicians may run only the two update commands as root, on any host (ALL). This is least privilege applied to administration.
  • g.lopez ALL=(ALL) ALL — the IT administrator may run any command as any user; this is what membership of the sudo group grants on Ubuntu.
  • sudo -l lists what the current account may run; NOPASSWD: removes the password prompt and is never used for a role account in this course.

Reference: man7.org — sudoers(5) and the project site sudo.ws. Direct login as root over SSH (Secure Shell) is disabled in LAB_03: administration goes through a named account and sudo, so that every action is attributable.

ModeSymbolicMeaning for a folderUsed for
2770drwxrws---Owner and group: everything; others: nothing; new files inherit the groupRole folders (client-records, techdocs, front-desk)
750drwxr-x---Group may enter and list, not writeRead-only reference folder for a role
700drwx------Owner onlyHome folders, SSH key folder
1777drwxrwxrwtEveryone writes; only the owner deletes its files/tmp
440-r--r-----File readable by owner and group onlyFiles in /etc/sudoers.d/

Real-life example — Create the three role folders on the Linux file server and restrict sudo for technicians

Task: Create client-records, techdocs and front-desk with root as owner and the role group as group, set mode 2770 on each, add a sudoers rule that limits technicians to the update commands, and prove the result with two tests: an accountant writes in client-records, the receptionist is refused.

Relation to the lecture: The script applies ownership, the octal mode with the setgid bit, and a least-privilege sudo rule; the two tests demonstrate the one-class evaluation rule (group class for the accountant, others class for the receptionist).

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: LAB_02 part 2 — folder permissions on Linux so that each role reaches only its own data, validated with the checklist; the sudo rule is reused in LAB_03 (host hardening: no root login, restricted administration). The ls -ld output and the two test lines are the evidence of Chapter 2, section N.4.

On the Linux file server of the laboratory, Gina creates /srv/northmaple with one sub-folder per role. Nobody works as root, so root is the owner and the role group is the group of each folder; mode 2770 gives everything to the group, nothing to others, and makes every new file inherit the group. The two technicians must be able to update the workstations without knowing the root password: a drop-in file in /etc/sudoers.d/ lets the group run apt update and apt upgrade as root, nothing else, and visudo -c checks the file before it is used. The validation runs two commands as two accounts: Alice creates a file in client-records (allowed); Farid tries to list client-records (Permission denied).

Deliverable of this example: Screenshots of ls -ld /srv/northmaple/*, of sudo -l run as a technician, and of the two validation tests — Chapter 2 of the manual.

Illustration script — nm_linux_permissions.sh (Bash (Linux))

Task: The script creates the role folders with the correct owner, group and mode 2770, installs a restricted sudoers rule for technicians, checks its syntax, and runs two access tests as two different accounts.

Relation to the lecture: It implements the Linux model of the lecture — owner, group, mode with setgid, one-class evaluation — and the sudo mechanism as controlled administrative access.

ready
#!/usr/bin/env bash# Stop at the first failing command, so that a folder is never left with the wrong mode.set -e # The base folder of the company data on the file server.BASE=/srv/northmaple # Create the base folder and one sub-folder per role (-p creates the parents and does not fail if a folder already exists).sudo mkdir -p $BASE/client-records $BASE/techdocs $BASE/front-desk # Ownership: root is the owner (nobody works as root), and the group is the role group that needs the folder.sudo chown root:accountants $BASE/client-recordssudo chown root:technicians $BASE/techdocssudo chown root:reception   $BASE/front-desk # Mode 2770: setgid (2) + owner rwx (7) + group rwx (7) + others nothing (0); new files inherit the group of the folder.sudo chmod 2770 $BASE/client-recordssudo chmod 2770 $BASE/techdocssudo chmod 2770 $BASE/front-desk # Evidence for the manual: the long listing shows drwxrws--- root <group> for each folder.ls -ld $BASE/* # sudo rule: members of technicians may run ONLY the two update commands as root (least privilege for administration).echo '%technicians ALL=(root) /usr/bin/apt update, /usr/bin/apt upgrade' | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/technicians > /dev/null # The files of sudoers.d must be readable by root and its group only, otherwise sudo refuses to use them.sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/technicians # Syntax check of the new rule file: a syntax error in sudoers locks everyone out of sudo, so the check is mandatory.sudo visudo -c -f /etc/sudoers.d/technicians # Validation 1: run one command as the accountant Alice - creating a file in client-records must succeed (group class: rwx).sudo -u a.tremblay touch $BASE/client-records/validation.txt && echo "accountant write to client-records: ALLOWED (correct)" # Validation 2: run one command as the receptionist Farid - listing client-records must fail (others class: ---).sudo -u f.haddad ls $BASE/client-records 2>/dev/null && echo "receptionist read of client-records: ALLOWED (WRONG)" || echo "receptionist read of client-records: DENIED (correct)"

Step-by-step explanation

  1. set -e and BASE prepare the script; every path is built from the one variable, which avoids typing errors.
  2. mkdir -p creates the base and the three role folders in one command.
  3. The three chown root:group lines set the owner to root and the group to the role group — the group is the only class that will hold rights.
  4. The three chmod 2770 lines set owner rwx, group rwx, others nothing, plus setgid so that every new file carries the group of the folder rather than the primary group of the person who created it.
  5. ls -ld $BASE/* prints the evidence line of each folder: drwxrws--- root accountants … client-records.
  6. The echo … | sudo tee line writes one sudoers rule into a drop-in file; %technicians designates a group, (root) the identity the commands run as, and the two full paths the only commands allowed.
  7. chmod 440 gives the drop-in file the mode sudo requires; visudo -c -f checks the syntax of that file only, before it is ever used.
  8. The two validation lines run one command as another account with sudo -u: the accountant's touch succeeds (group class), the receptionist's ls fails (others class) and the || branch prints the expected denial.
  9. Run it with chmod +x nm_linux_permissions.sh then ./nm_linux_permissions.sh, after the identities of section 1.3 exist.

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

What are the values of r, w and x, and what is rwx in octal?
r = 4, w = 2, x = 1; rwx = 7.
What does the x bit mean on a folder?
The right to enter the folder and reach its entries; r alone lists the names without giving access to them.
What does the setgid bit do on a folder?
New files and sub-folders inherit the group of the folder instead of the primary group of their creator.
Which class of bits applies to a subject?
Only one: the owner bits if the subject is the owner, otherwise the group bits if the subject is a member of the group, otherwise the others bits. There is no cumulation.
Why must sudoers files be edited with visudo?
visudo checks the syntax before saving; a syntax error in a sudoers file locks everyone out of sudo.

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. What is the octal mode of a file shown as -rw-r-----?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Owner rw-, group r--, others ---.

✓ 640 — Correct: rw- = 6, r-- = 4, --- = 0.

✗ 644 — 644 would give others read (r--).

✗ 750 — 750 would give the owner execute and the group read and execute.

✗ 600 — 600 would give the group nothing.

Q2. A file is owned by root:accountants with mode 660. What can b.nguyen, a member of accountants, do with it?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Which class applies to a group member who is not the owner?

✗ Nothing. — The group class gives rw-.

✓ Read and write. — Correct: the group class (6 = rw-) applies; there is no execute bit.

✗ Execute it. — No class has the x bit.

✗ Change its owner. — Changing the owner requires root.

Q3. Why is mode 2770 preferred to 770 on a team folder?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The leading 2 is a special bit.

✗ The 2 makes the folder read-only. — The leading digit carries special bits; it does not remove rights.

✓ The setgid bit makes new files inherit the group of the folder. — Correct: without it, a file created by a.tremblay would carry her primary group and other accountants could be refused.

✗ The 2 gives others read access. — Others keep 0 in both modes.

✗ The 2 is the sticky bit. — The sticky bit is 1; setgid is 2; setuid is 4.

Q4. What does the rule %technicians ALL=(root) /usr/bin/apt update mean?one answer — 4 options

Hint: who where=(as_whom) commands; % designates a group.

✗ Technicians may run any command as root. — Only the listed command is allowed.

✓ Members of the group technicians may run apt update as root, on any host. — Correct: % = group, ALL = any host, (root) = run as root, then the one allowed command.

✗ The user named technicians becomes root. — % designates a group, not a user, and sudo never changes who the person is.

✗ apt is disabled for technicians. — The rule allows, it does not deny.

Q5. Which of the following are special permission bits? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Three bits carried by the leading octal digit.

✓ setuid — Value 4: a program runs with the identity of its owner.

✓ setgid — Value 2: on a folder, new files inherit the group.

✓ sticky bit — Value 1: only the owner of a file may delete it in a shared folder.

✗ read — r is an ordinary permission bit.

✗ inherit — Inheritance flags are an NTFS (New Technology File System) concept.

✗ deny — Basic Linux modes have no Deny entry; refusal comes from the absence of bits.

Q6. Which statements about the Linux permission check are true? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: One class, no cumulation, root is special, ACLs exist for exceptions.

✓ Only one class of bits is evaluated for a given subject. — Owner, else group, else others.

✓ root bypasses the read and write checks. — root reads and writes any file; execution still needs an x bit.

✗ Rights cumulate across the owner and the group classes. — There is no cumulation: the first matching class decides.

✓ The others class applies to accounts that are neither the owner nor members of the group. — That is the definition of the others class.

✗ A Deny entry exists in the basic mode bits. — Refusal comes from absent bits; explicit Deny is an NTFS concept.

✓ POSIX ACLs (setfacl) can add an exception for one extra user. — Awareness level: getfacl and setfacl extend the basic model.

2.3 Techniques for securing access to sensitive data and systems 8 min

Slides 34–38 of the deck — 34 2.3 Securing access to sensitive data (1/2); 35 2.3 Securing access to sensitive data (2/2); 36 2.3 The lockout policy, as a number; 37 2.3 Layers around the client records; 38 2.3 Example — Harden-AccountAccess.ps1
Slide 34Slide 35Slide 36Slide 37Slide 38

Sensitive data is the information whose loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability — the three properties of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad — causes damage to the organization or to the people it concerns. At NorthMaple, the client financial records are confidential; the technical documentation is internal; the public website is public. The data classification decides which techniques below apply to which folder, and how strictly. The techniques are grouped by the process they protect.

  1. Stronger authentication. A password policy with a minimum length of 12 characters, no reuse of the last passwords, and a maximum age; MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) with a TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) code from an authenticator application for every remote or administrative access (the VPN (Virtual Private Network) of LAB_06 and the management interface of the firewall of LAB_05 support TOTP); SSH (Secure Shell) keys instead of passwords for Linux administration (LAB_03).
  2. Account lockout and rate limiting. After a small number of wrong passwords (5), the account is locked for a fixed duration (15 minutes). On Windows this is the lockout policy; on Linux, pam_faillock; for services exposed to the network, fail2ban. The effect is measurable: without lockout, an attacker who tries one password per second can make 86 400 attempts per day on one account; with 5 attempts per 15 minutes, the maximum is 480 — row 2 of the resilience assessment.
  3. Privileged account separation. One named administrative account per administrator, used only for administrative tasks; the built-in Administrator account disabled or renamed; no shared accounts; UAC (User Account Control) and sudo as the only paths to elevation.
  4. Authorization by role. Least privilege and need-to-know through groups: NTFS (New Technology File System) Modify for the role, mode 2770 on Linux, nothing for the other roles (sections 1.2, 2.1, 2.2).
  5. Protection of the data itself. Encryption at rest (BitLocker on Windows, LUKS on Linux, VeraCrypt as a portable open-source option — LAB_06) so that a stolen disk or laptop reveals nothing (row 5); encryption in transit (SMB (Server Message Block) signing and encryption on the share, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), VPN) so that an interception reveals nothing (row 6).
  6. Monitoring of access. Auditing entries (SACL (System Access Control List)) on the sensitive folder and the failed-logon events on Windows; auditd and the authentication log on Linux; a review of the failed logons at each access review; the IDS (Intrusion Detection System) of LAB_04 for the network side. Detection is the layer that tells the organization that the other layers are being tested.
  7. Availability of the data. Backups following the 3-2-1 rule — three copies, on two different media, one of them off-site or offline — restored at least once to prove they work (row 10, ransomware).
  8. Hygiene of the systems. Screen lock after inactivity, session time-outs, security updates (LAB_03), removal of unused services and accounts (section 1.4).

These techniques are the baseline that the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security recommends to small and medium organizations (cyber.gc.ca — Baseline cyber security controls) and that the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls organize in Controls 3 (Data Protection), 4 (Secure Configuration), 5 and 6.

Real-life example — Apply the account policies and the auditing that protect the ClientRecords folder

Task: On the Windows file server of the laboratory, set the password policy and the lockout policy, create a separate administrative account for the IT administrator, remove administrative rights from her daily account, enable auditing of the client-records folder, and display the resulting policy as evidence.

Relation to the lecture: The script applies techniques 1, 2, 3 and 6 of the list: authentication strength, lockout, privileged account separation and monitoring. The runner shows the measurable effect of the lockout on the number of password attempts per day.

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: LAB_03 part 1 — the hardening checklist for the Windows host (account and security policies) with before-and-after evidence; the separate administrative account completes LAB_02; the auditing entries prepare the log review of LAB_04. Rows 2 and 9 of the resilience assessment cite these policies.

The remote access of NorthMaple will be tested by password guessing: it is scenario 2 of the resilience assessment. Before the VPN exists, Gina applies the policies on the file server: passwords of 12 characters minimum, no reuse of the last five, lockout after 5 failures for 15 minutes. She creates g.lopez-adm, tests a login with it, then removes her daily account g.lopez from Administrators. Finally she enables auditing of failed access attempts on the client-records folder, so that a refused attempt by another role appears in the security log. The net accounts output before and after is the evidence of the hardening checklist.

Deliverable of this example: Before-and-after screenshots of net accounts, a screenshot of the Administrators group (daily account absent, administrative account present), and one audit event from the security log — LAB_03 checklist and Chapter 3 of the manual.

Illustration script — Harden-AccountAccess.ps1 (PowerShell (Windows))

Task: The script sets the local password and lockout policies, creates a separate administrative account, removes administrative rights from the daily account, enables auditing on the client-records folder, and prints the policy in force.

Relation to the lecture: It implements four of the eight techniques of the lecture (authentication strength, lockout, privileged account separation, monitoring) on the Windows host of the laboratory.

ready
# Stop at the first error, so that no policy is left half-applied.$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop" # Evidence BEFORE: display the account policies currently in force (this output is the "before" screenshot of the hardening checklist).net accounts # Technique 1 - Password policy: minimum length 12, maximum age 90 days, the last 5 passwords cannot be reused (net accounts applies to local accounts).net accounts /minpwlen:12 /maxpwage:90 /uniquepw:5 # Technique 2 - Lockout policy: 5 wrong passwords lock the account for 15 minutes; the failure counter resets after 15 minutes without failure.net accounts /lockoutthreshold:5 /lockoutduration:15 /lockoutwindow:15 # Technique 3 - A separate administrative account for the IT administrator, with a laboratory-only password typed at the prompt (never written in a script).New-LocalUser -Name "g.lopez-adm" -FullName "Gina Lopez (administrative account)" -Password (Read-Host -AsSecureString "Laboratory-only password for g.lopez-adm") | Out-Null # The administrative account joins the Administrators group; it is used only for administrative tasks.Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "g.lopez-adm" # The daily account leaves the Administrators group: e-mail and documents never run with administrative rights (do this only after a test logon of g.lopez-adm succeeded).Remove-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "g.lopez" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue # The built-in Administrator account is disabled: attackers know its name, and a named account gives attribution (it is already disabled by default on Windows 10 and 11).Disable-LocalUser -Name "Administrator" # Technique 6 - Auditing: enable the recording of successful and failed file-system access attempts in the security log.auditpol /set /subcategory:"File System" /success:enable /failure:enable # The folder whose access attempts must be recorded.$Folder = "D:\NorthMaple\ClientRecords" # Read the current security descriptor of the folder (the SACL will be modified, the DACL of section 2.1 stays unchanged).$acl = Get-Acl $Folder # Build one auditing entry: record every FAILED attempt by anyone (Everyone) to read, write or delete data, for the folder, its files and its sub-folders.$rule = New-Object System.Security.AccessControl.FileSystemAuditRule("Everyone", "ReadData,WriteData,Delete", "ContainerInherit,ObjectInherit", "None", "Failure") # Add the auditing entry to the SACL held in memory.$acl.AddAuditRule($rule) # Write the modified security descriptor back to the folder.Set-Acl -Path $Folder -AclObject $acl # Evidence AFTER: display the account policies now in force (the "after" screenshot of the hardening checklist).net accounts

Step-by-step explanation

  1. The first net accounts prints the current policy: this is the before evidence required by the LAB_03 checklist.
  2. net accounts /minpwlen:12 /maxpwage:90 /uniquepw:5 sets the password policy of the local machine; in a domain the same values are set in a GPO (Group Policy Object).
  3. net accounts /lockoutthreshold:5 /lockoutduration:15 /lockoutwindow:15 sets the lockout policy: threshold, duration of the lock, and observation window.
  4. New-LocalUser g.lopez-adm creates the administrative account; the password is typed at the prompt, so that no password is ever stored in a script.
  5. Add-LocalGroupMember Administrators g.lopez-adm then Remove-LocalGroupMember Administrators g.lopez move the administrative rights from the daily account to the administrative one; the order matters, and a test logon of the new account is required before the removal.
  6. Disable-LocalUser Administrator disables the built-in account whose name every attacker knows.
  7. auditpol /set … enables the audit category; without it, SACL entries record nothing.
  8. The Get-Acl, FileSystemAuditRule, AddAuditRule, Set-Acl sequence adds one SACL entry that records every failed read, write or delete attempt on the folder and its content.
  9. The last net accounts prints the after evidence. Run the script in an elevated session; each step can also be done in the graphical Local Security Policy console (secpol.msc).

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

What is MFA?
Authentication with two or more independent factors — something the person knows (password), has (authenticator application, hardware key), or is (biometrics).
What is the maximum number of password attempts per day on one account with a lockout of 5 attempts per 15 minutes?
480 (5 attempts × 96 windows of 15 minutes), against 86 400 at one attempt per second without lockout.
Why does an administrator use two accounts?
The daily account holds no privileges, so that no program started during daily work — including a malicious attachment — runs with administrative rights.
Encryption at rest versus encryption in transit: which lab applies each?
At rest (BitLocker, LUKS, VeraCrypt) and in transit (VPN (Virtual Private Network), HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)): both in LAB_06.
State the 3-2-1 backup rule.
Three copies of the data, on two different media, one copy off-site or offline — and a tested restore.

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. Which control limits password guessing against the VPN of NorthMaple?one answer — 4 options

Hint: It acts on the number of attempts.

✗ NTFS Modify on the client-records folder. — A folder permission does not limit authentication attempts.

✓ Account lockout or rate limiting. — Correct: 5 attempts per 15 minutes reduce 86 400 daily attempts to 480.

✗ The setgid bit. — setgid concerns the group of new files.

✗ Share permissions. — Share permissions apply after authentication.

Q2. What does MFA mean?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Independent factors, not several instances of the same factor.

✗ Two different passwords. — Two passwords are two instances of the same factor (something known).

✓ Two or more independent authentication factors. — Correct: know, have, are.

✗ A password longer than 16 characters. — Length strengthens one factor; it does not add another.

✗ Fingerprint only. — One factor only, of the 'are' type.

Q3. What does a SACL entry do?one answer — 4 options

Hint: The S stands for System, and the list concerns the security log.

✗ It grants access to the folder. — Access decisions are in the DACL (Discretionary Access Control List).

✓ It records access attempts in the security log. — Correct: auditing entries define which successes or failures are logged.

✗ It encrypts the folder. — Encryption is a separate mechanism (BitLocker, EFS (Encrypting File System)).

✗ It shares the folder on the network. — Sharing is done with New-SmbShare.

Q4. What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Copies, media, location.

✗ Three backups per day. — The rule concerns copies, media and location, not frequency.

✓ Three copies, on two different media, one of them off-site or offline. — Correct — and the restore must be tested.

✗ Three administrators check two backups once. — Not a backup rule.

✗ Three passwords, two factors, one account. — Not a backup rule.

Q5. Which of the following are authentication controls? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Authentication proves the identity; authorization decides what it may do.

✓ A minimum password length policy. — Strengthens the knowledge factor.

✓ MFA with a TOTP code. — Adds a possession factor.

✓ SSH keys instead of passwords. — A stronger knowledge/possession factor for administration.

✗ NTFS Modify for the Accountants group. — Authorization, not authentication.

✗ Mode 2770 on a role folder. — Authorization, not authentication.

✓ An account lockout policy. — It protects the authentication process against guessing.

Q6. Which measures belong to the protection of the client records on the file server? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Look for measures that protect confidentiality, integrity or availability of that folder.

✓ Least-privilege permissions on the folder. — Confidentiality and integrity through authorization.

✓ Encryption of the volume that holds the folder. — Confidentiality of the data at rest.

✓ Tested backups of the folder. — Availability, including after ransomware.

✓ Audit entries on the folder. — Detection of refused or unexpected access.

✗ Disabling the host firewall to speed up file sharing. — Removes a layer; it protects nothing.

✗ One shared 'accounting' account with a strong password for all accountants. — A shared account removes attribution and cannot be reviewed.

2.4 Malware families that abuse weak access control — backdoors, Trojans, rootkits, worms, bots and botnets — and basic detection and prevention 10 min

Slides 39–42 of the deck — 39 2.4 Malware families that abuse weak access control (1/2); 40 2.4 Detection and prevention (2/2); 41 2.4 The weakness each family abuses, and the layer that answers; 42 2.4 Example — nm_integrity_check.py
Slide 39Slide 40Slide 41Slide 42

Malware is software written to perform actions that the owner of the system did not authorize. Every family below needs access — a permission it should not have, a privilege it should not hold, an account it should not know — and each family abuses a different weakness of access control. Defense therefore starts with the previous four sections. Classification and technique references: MITRE ATT&CK (the knowledge base of adversary techniques; ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is its name) and the guidance of the CISA (CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency)).

FamilyDefinitionWeakness of access control abusedBasic detectionBasic prevention
BackdoorA hidden way to access a system that bypasses normal authentication: an added account, a listening service, a modified service, a scheduled task that reopens the access.Administrative rights obtained by the attacker; absence of account and service reviews.Unexpected accounts or group members (access review), unexpected listening ports (ss -tlnp, netstat -ano), unknown scheduled tasks and startup entries.Least privilege, access reviews, host firewall (LAB_03), integrity baseline.
TrojanA program that presents itself as legitimate (an invoice, an installer, a game) and performs hidden actions when the user runs it.The user runs it with a daily account that holds administrative rights.Antivirus and EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) alerts, unusual processes, unexpected outbound connections.No administrative rights for daily work, application control, attachment filtering, user awareness.
RootkitSoftware that hides its own presence by modifying the operating system: replaced system binaries (ps, ls, netstat), kernel modules, drivers.Administrative or kernel privileges, obtained through weak privilege separation or an unpatched vulnerability.File integrity check against a baseline of hashes (the example below), offline scanning from a clean system, rkhunter and chkrootkit on Linux, Secure Boot.Least privilege, security updates, signed drivers, Secure Boot.
WormA self-replicating program that spreads across the network without user action, by exploiting a vulnerable service or by writing copies into accessible shares.Shares writable by Everyone, reused administrative passwords, unpatched services reachable across zones.IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alerts (LAB_04), traffic spikes between machines, many failed logons in the logs.Security updates, network zoning (LAB_01, LAB_05), host firewalls (LAB_03), least privilege on shares.
Bot and botnetA bot is an infected machine controlled remotely through a C2 (Command and Control) channel; a botnet is a group of bots under one controller, used for DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service) attacks, spam, or password guessing against other organizations.Persistence obtained through administrative rights; default credentials left on network devices (row 9).Periodic outbound connections to unknown hosts in the firewall and IDS logs; unexpected processes that start at boot.Changing default credentials (LAB_05), outbound filtering on the firewall, updates, least privilege.

Ransomware combines these behaviors: delivered like a Trojan, sometimes spreading like a worm, it encrypts every file the compromised account can write to (row 10). Its reach is bounded by the same rule as in section 1.2: the permissions of the account that runs it. When least privilege blocks a family, the attacker's next step is privilege escalation — obtaining higher rights through a vulnerability or a misconfiguration; this is why security updates (LAB_03) belong to access control. Technique references in ATT&CK: T1078 Valid Accounts, T1014 Rootkit, T1110 Brute Force.

Detection tools available at no cost: Microsoft Defender Antivirus on Windows (Microsoft Learn — Defender Antivirus), ClamAV on Linux, a file integrity baseline built with sha256sum or Get-FileHash (Class 14 practises hashing), the Snort or Suricata sensor of LAB_04, and the log review of section 1.4. Prevention, in order of effect: least privilege (sections 1.2 to 2.2), security updates, host firewalls, changed default credentials, tested backups.

Legal reminder (Legal Notice, sections 3 and 4). Students never create, install, or release malicious software outside the isolated laboratory, and never against a system they do not own. The example of this section is a detection tool; it contains no malware, and the "modified" files of the demonstration are simulated by the runner, not produced by any attack.

Real-life example — Build a file integrity baseline of the Linux file server and detect a modified system binary

Task: Record the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) hash of the critical files of the server (system binaries, account files, sudo rules, scheduled tasks), then compare the current hashes with the baseline one week later and report every file that changed or disappeared.

Relation to the lecture: A rootkit replaces system binaries and a backdoor adds a scheduled task; both change the hash of a file that should not change. The baseline is the detection measure of the table for these two families, and it works only if the baseline is stored where the compromised account cannot rewrite it.

Relation to the labs and the Final Project: LAB_03 — the before-and-after evidence of hardening uses the same hashing technique; Class 14 practises hashing with OpenSSL; LAB_04 adds network detection; rows 1, 4 and 10 of the resilience assessment cite integrity checks and backups. Students may reuse this script as their own helper tool (with disclosure in the manual).

Gina builds a baseline of six critical files right after the hardening of LAB_03 and stores it on a separate, read-only medium. One week later, the check reports two changes: /usr/bin/ps and /etc/crontab. A modified ps is the signature of a rootkit that hides processes; a modified crontab is the signature of a backdoor that restarts itself. The other four files are unchanged. The response is not to repair the two files but to isolate the machine, restore it from a clean snapshot or backup, and rotate the credentials — the procedure written in Chapter 7. In the laboratory, the two changes are simulated by the runner; no file is ever modified by an attack.

Deliverable of this example: The baseline file (northmaple_baseline.json) stored off the machine, the check output with two CHANGED lines, and the response procedure — LAB_03 evidence and Chapter 7 of the manual.

Illustration script — nm_integrity_check.py (Python 3)

Task: The script computes the SHA-256 hash of a list of critical files. With the argument init it stores the hashes as a baseline; without argument it recomputes them and reports OK, CHANGED, or MISSING for every file.

Relation to the lecture: It is the detection measure of the malware table for rootkits (replaced binaries) and backdoors (modified scheduled tasks): a change of hash in a file that must not change.

ready
# hashlib computes the SHA-256 hash; json stores the baseline; os checks that files exist; sys reads the command-line argument.import hashlib, json, os, sys # The critical files of the Linux server: system binaries a rootkit replaces, account and sudo files a backdoor edits, and the scheduled tasks it uses to restart.WATCHED = ["/usr/bin/ls", "/usr/bin/ps", "/usr/bin/ss", "/etc/passwd", "/etc/sudoers", "/etc/crontab"] # The baseline file: it must be stored on a separate, read-only medium, so that an attacker cannot rewrite it together with the files.BASELINE_FILE = "northmaple_baseline.json" # A function that returns the SHA-256 hash of one file, read in blocks of 64 KiB so that large files do not fill the memory.def sha256(path):    # The hash object that accumulates the content of the file.    h = hashlib.sha256()    # Open the file in binary mode: a hash is computed on bytes, never on decoded text.    with open(path, "rb") as f:        # Read block after block until the file ends, feeding each block to the hash object.        for block in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):            h.update(block)    # Return the 64-character hexadecimal representation of the hash.    return h.hexdigest() # Build the baseline: compute the hash of every watched file that exists and store the result as JSON.def build_baseline():    # A dictionary path -> hash, for the files that exist on this machine.    baseline = {p: sha256(p) for p in WATCHED if os.path.exists(p)}    # Write the dictionary to the baseline file in a readable format.    with open(BASELINE_FILE, "w") as f:        json.dump(baseline, f, indent=2)    # Confirm how many files are now protected by the baseline.    print(f"Baseline created for {len(baseline)} files -> {BASELINE_FILE}") # Check the machine against the baseline: recompute every hash and compare it with the stored value.def check():    # Load the stored hashes.    with open(BASELINE_FILE) as f:        baseline = json.load(f)    # Compare file after file and print a verdict for each.    for path, old_hash in baseline.items():        # A file that disappeared is reported as MISSING; otherwise its current hash is computed.        new_hash = sha256(path) if os.path.exists(path) else None        # Same hash: unchanged; different hash: changed and must be investigated; None: missing.        status = "OK" if new_hash == old_hash else ("MISSING" if new_hash is None else "CHANGED - investigate")        print(f"{status:22} {path}") # Entry point: "init" builds the baseline; any other call runs the check.if __name__ == "__main__":    build_baseline() if sys.argv[1:] == ["init"] else check()

Step-by-step explanation

  1. The four imports give hashing (hashlib), storage (json), file tests (os) and the command-line argument (sys).
  2. WATCHED lists the files that must never change silently: three binaries, two access control files, one scheduler file. Students may add the files of their own server.
  3. BASELINE_FILE names the stored baseline. The comment states the essential condition: the baseline is stored where a compromised account cannot rewrite it.
  4. sha256() reads the file in blocks and returns its hash; the hash changes if a single byte of the file changes.
  5. build_baseline() hashes every existing watched file and writes the dictionary to the baseline file — this is run once, right after hardening.
  6. check() loads the baseline, recomputes every hash, and prints OK, CHANGED or MISSING per file; CHANGED on a system binary is the rootkit indicator, CHANGED on crontab the backdoor indicator.
  7. The entry point selects the mode: sudo python3 nm_integrity_check.py init creates the baseline; sudo python3 nm_integrity_check.py checks. sudo is needed to read /etc/sudoers.
  8. The response to a CHANGED line is a procedure, not a repair: isolate, restore from a clean snapshot, rotate credentials, document (Chapter 7).

Flash cards — click a card to flip it

What is the difference between a Trojan and a worm?
A Trojan needs the user to run it and holds the rights of that user; a worm spreads by itself across the network through vulnerable services or writable shares.
Which privilege level does a rootkit need, and which two measures prevent it?
Administrative or kernel privileges; least privilege (no administrative rights for daily work) and security updates.
What is a backdoor, and where does one look for it?
A hidden access that bypasses authentication; look at unexpected accounts and group members, listening ports, scheduled tasks and startup entries.
What is a botnet and how is a bot detected?
A group of infected machines controlled through a command-and-control channel; a bot is detected by periodic outbound connections to unknown hosts in the firewall and IDS (Intrusion Detection System) logs.
How does a file integrity baseline work?
Hash the critical files once and store the hashes on a read-only medium; recompute later and investigate every file whose hash changed or that disappeared.

Self-check quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

Q1. Which malware family spreads across the network without any user action?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Self-replication is its defining property.

✗ Trojan. — A Trojan needs the user to run it.

✓ Worm. — Correct: it copies itself through vulnerable services or writable shares.

✗ Rootkit. — A rootkit hides a presence; it does not spread by itself.

✗ Backdoor. — A backdoor is an access path, not a propagation mechanism.

Q2. The hash of /usr/bin/ps changed and the tool no longer shows some processes. What is the most likely family?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Hiding the presence of processes by replacing system binaries.

✗ Worm. — A worm spreads; it does not primarily modify system tools to hide.

✓ Rootkit. — Correct: replaced system binaries that hide processes are the signature of a rootkit.

✗ Botnet. — A bot communicates with a controller; it may use a rootkit, but the replaced binary itself is the rootkit.

✗ Spam. — Spam is unwanted e-mail, not a malware family.

Q3. Which weakness lets a worm write copies of itself into a shared folder?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Think about who may write on the share.

✓ Share or NTFS permissions that give Everyone Write. — Correct: a share writable by any identity accepts the copies of the worm.

✗ Mode 2770 on the folder. — 2770 limits writing to the group; others cannot write.

✗ An account lockout policy. — Lockout concerns authentication attempts.

✗ MFA on the VPN. — MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) concerns remote authentication.

Q4. A workstation connects every ten minutes to an unknown server abroad, at night. What is this most likely?one answer — 4 options

Hint: Regular outbound connections to an unknown host.

✗ A backup job. — Backups go to a known destination defined by the company.

✓ A command-and-control communication of a bot. — Correct: periodic outbound connections to unknown hosts are the detection signal for bots.

✗ A security update. — Updates come from known vendor servers, on a schedule the administrator knows.

✗ A DNS query. — A DNS (Domain Name System) query goes to the configured resolver, not to an unknown server abroad.

Q5. Which measures prevent a Trojan from installing a rootkit? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: A rootkit needs privileges the Trojan must obtain first.

✓ No administrative rights for daily work. — The Trojan runs with the user's rights and cannot modify system files.

✓ Security updates applied on time. — They remove the vulnerabilities used for privilege escalation.

✓ UAC and sudo prompts for elevation. — Elevation is explicit and attributable instead of permanent.

✗ A larger hard disk. — Disk size has no effect on access control.

✗ Everyone: Full control on the system folder. — This is the weakness the rootkit needs.

✓ Antivirus or EDR software. — Detection and blocking of known Trojans before execution.

Q6. Which of the following are detection measures? (choose all that apply)select all that apply — 6 options

Hint: Detection tells the organization that something happened; it does not by itself stop it.

✓ A file integrity baseline compared at fixed intervals. — Detects replaced binaries and modified configuration files.

✓ IDS alerts on the network. — LAB_04.

✓ A review of accounts, group members and listening ports. — Detects backdoors.

✓ An antivirus scan. — Detects known malware.

✗ Disabling the security log to save disk space. — This removes detection.

✗ Disabling the host firewall. — This removes a prevention layer and detects nothing.

Lesson 2 — checkpoint

Five sentences to remember

  1. NTFS (New Technology File System): rights are cumulative, Deny wins, explicit beats inherited, absence means no access, inheritance propagates; through a share, the more restrictive of share and NTFS applies.
  2. Linux: owner, group, others; r = 4, w = 2, x = 1; one class decides; 2770 for a role folder; sudo rules edited with visudo only.
  3. Eight techniques secure sensitive data, each attached to the process it protects; a lockout policy turns 86 400 attempts per day into 480.
  4. Backdoors, Trojans, rootkits, worms, bots and botnets each need an access they should not have; detection tells you the layers are being tested.
  5. Every mechanism of today is applied in LAB_02 and reused in LAB_03.

Objective. Implement, on one Windows machine and one Linux machine of your isolated laboratory, the role table of NorthMaple Accounting Inc.: users, groups, least-privilege memberships, and folder permissions — then prove with test logins that each role reaches only its own data.

Part 1 — today's supervised work time

  • Start from the laboratory environment of LAB_01 (VirtualBox, or a personal free-tier account on AWS (Amazon Web Services) or Microsoft Azure): one Windows machine and one Linux machine, both with a snapshot taken before you begin.
  • Create the four role groups and the seven staff accounts on each machine, following the role table (section 1.3). The scripts nm_identities.sh and nm_identities.ps1 of this lecture are accepted starting points — adapt them and state it in the manual.
  • Apply least-privilege memberships: one role group per account; technicians are local administrators of the workstations only; the IT administrator uses a separate administrative account (section 2.3).
  • Verify with simple test logins that each role can access only what it needs, and take one screenshot per test.

Part 2 — to finish before the LAB_02 deadline

  • Create the role folders (ClientRecords, TechDocs, FrontDesk) on each machine: NTFS (New Technology File System) and share permissions on Windows (section 2.1), ownership and mode 2770 on Linux (section 2.2).
  • Run the provided validation checklist: for each role, one allowed access and one refused access, with screenshots.
  • Deliverable: the completed permission tables and validation screenshots — this becomes the access-control chapter (Chapter 2) of the Final Project and of the Course Procedure Manual.
  • Write Chapter 2 of the manual this week, following the standard chapter template (objective, environment, numbered steps, validation, problems met, AI (Artificial Intelligence) disclosure).

Evidence expected in the submission

  • Practice only inside your personal, isolated laboratory environment, as defined in LAB_01: a local virtualization tool (for example VirtualBox) or your own personal free-tier cloud account on AWS (Amazon Web Services) or Microsoft Azure.
  • Practice on any other system only if you hold explicit written permission from the owner of that system, obtained before you start.
  • Use snapshots and isolated virtual networks so that a mistake stays inside your laboratory.

You must never:

  • Scan, probe, attack, intercept, monitor, or access any system, network, wireless network, or account that is not yours — including those of the college, an employer, a business, a public website, or a neighbor.
  • Create, install, or release malicious software outside your isolated laboratory.
  • Attempt password, credential, or interception attacks against any real account or any real communication.
  • Use the Material, or any tool presented in it, to break any law or any policy that applies to you.

Cloud responsibilities: if you use a cloud account, you must respect the acceptable-use policies of the provider (AWS or Microsoft Azure). Free tiers have limits; monitor them. All cloud costs, overage charges, and account consequences are your responsibility.

4. Legal Warning

Unauthorized computer access or use is a criminal offence. In Canada, the Criminal Code contains, among other provisions: section 342.1 (unauthorized use of a computer), section 342.2 (possession of a device to obtain unauthorized use of a computer), and section 430(1.1) (mischief in relation to computer data). Penalties can include imprisonment. If you are located outside Canada, the laws of your own country, province, or state apply to you, and you must know and obey them. The policies and codes of conduct of your college apply in addition to the law. The instructor never asks for, and never authorizes, any illegal act. If an activity seems to touch a system you do not own, stop and ask the instructor before doing anything.
